items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Midland, TX
items.meta: Midland mineral owner? We buy Spraberry and Wolfcamp interests directly, reading your division order and nearby permits before quoting a number, no listing needed.

sections.html:
Midland is the town the basin is named after in everyone's mind, and owning minerals under or near it usually means sitting on some of the most-drilled acreage in the country.

Most Midland mineral tracts we look at trace to the same Spraberry and Wolfcamp development that's made this county the operational center of the whole Permian. Some interests here have been producing since the original Spraberry discovery in 1949, since re-completed and re-drilled with horizontal wells over the last decade and a half.

sections.title: City growth versus mineral ownership
sections.html: Midland has expanded a lot over the years, and plenty of mineral tracts that were open ranchland when the reservation was written now sit under subdivisions, office parks, or the airport corridor. That doesn't change your ownership under Texas law, mineral and surface estates stay separate, though it can complicate future drilling access on some sections.

sections.title: What we check before quoting
sections.html: We pull your division order alongside the Railroad Commission history for every wellbore on your unit, since a lot of Midland tracts have several stacked Wolfcamp benches producing under one surface location. We also check for recent permits on offset sections, given how much active development still runs through this county.

sections.title: Why buyer competition is stronger here
sections.html: Because Midland is where so many operators and mineral buyers are based, owners here tend to get more unsolicited offer letters than owners in surrounding counties. That's actually useful for you, more competition among buyers generally means it's worth comparing offers rather than settling for the first number that arrives.

sections.title: Begin with the county record trail

sections.title: Route local legal and tax questions correctly

sections.title: Read the local tract against the Permian schedule

The review pairs the legal description with producing wells, product lines, paid decimals, deductions, check history, decline, nearby permits, offset completions, operator changes, title exceptions, retained depths, and the exact property schedule in the written offer. Observed payments and recorded interests stay distinct from possible future locations, marketing claims, and assumptions that still need dated support.

faqs.q: Does it matter that your minerals are under the city now instead of open land?
faqs.a: Not for ownership. Texas law keeps mineral and surface estates separate regardless of surface development, though it can affect future drilling access on some built-up tracts.

faqs.q: How do you handle a tract with several wells on it?
faqs.a: We pull production history for every wellbore tied to your unit, since Midland acreage commonly has multiple Wolfcamp benches and the Spraberry stacked together.

faqs.q: How fast can a Midland sale close?
faqs.a: Typically two to four weeks with clean title and a current division order. Interests needing heirship or title work take longer, and we'll be upfront about that timeline.

faqs.q: Why do you get so many unsolicited offer letters for your Midland minerals?
faqs.a: This county has more mineral buyers active than most surrounding counties, given how much operator activity and headquarters presence there is here. It's worth comparing multiple offers before deciding who to sell to.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Midland County, TX/NM
items.meta: Midland County is the operational heart of the basin, home to the Spraberry Trend and the operators who drill it. We buy mineral and royalty interests here directly.

sections.html:
Midland County is where most of the companies drilling the rest of the basin keep their offices, and that changes how mineral interests here get bought and sold.

We spent a good stretch of our career in Midland, and if you own minerals in this county you're sitting under one of the most studied pieces of rock in American oil and gas history. The Spraberry Trend was discovered here in 1949 and turned out to be one of the largest oil fields by surface area in the country, and decades later the same acreage got a second life once operators figured out how to landing horizontal wells in the Wolfcamp benches underneath it.

That long history is exactly why Midland County mineral ownership gets complicated. You might have an interest tracing back to a 1950s vertical lease that's been assigned, re-assigned, and split among heirs three or four times since, sitting under a section that now has modern horizontal wells stacked on top of the old vertical bores. We sort out which production you're actually entitled to before we quote anything.

sections.title: Stacked pay changes how your interest should be valued
sections.html:
Midland County acreage typically has several productive intervals stacked on top of each other, the Spraberry itself along with the Wolfcamp A, B, and lower benches, sometimes the Dean and Jo Mill zones too. A tract that looks unremarkable based on one old vertical well might have three or four modern horizontal wells targeting different depths beneath it, each with its own spacing unit and division order.

This is where a lot of owners get shortchanged by buyers who price off a single well rather than checking every zone. We pull the full wellbore history against your tract across all producing intervals rather than whichever single well happens to be paying you right now.

sections.title: Being close to headquarters cuts both ways
sections.html:
Because so many operators are headquartered in Midland, permitting and development activity here tends to be well documented and fast-moving, which is good for owners wanting current information about their acreage. It also means Midland County land and mineral prices get more attention and more competing buyers than a lot of surrounding counties.

That's a point in your favor as a seller, but it also means it pays to get more than one number before deciding. We'll show you our reasoning, based on your specific production history and nearby permits, so you can judge our offer against anything else you've received.

sections.title: Urban growth and mineral estates
sections.html:
Midland itself has grown enough that some mineral tracts in the county now sit under developed residential or commercial surface. That doesn't change your mineral ownership, Texas law keeps the mineral and surface estates separate, but it can affect access for future drilling on some of the more built-up sections near town.

If your family's minerals came down through a ranching or farming operation that predates the city's growth, we're used to reconstructing that history from courthouse deed records even when the current surface bears no resemblance to what it looked like when the mineral reservation was first made.

faqs.q: How do you value a tract with multiple stacked pay zones?
faqs.a: We pull the full production and permit history for every interval under your tract instead of only the well currently paying you, since Midland County acreage commonly has several productive zones like the Spraberry and multiple Wolfcamp benches stacked beneath one surface location.

faqs.q: Does it matter that operators are headquartered in Midland?
faqs.a: It generally means more documented, faster-moving activity and more competing buyers for acreage here, which can work in your favor. We encourage owners to compare offers before deciding.

faqs.q: your minerals are under a developed part of Midland now. Can they still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Surface development doesn't change mineral ownership under Texas law, though it can affect future drilling access on some built-up sections. We'll flag anything relevant to your specific tract.

faqs.q: your family's lease dates back to the 1950s Spraberry discovery era. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: Not for us. We regularly trace chain of title through decades of assignments and heirship on older Midland County leases using county clerk deed records.

faqs.q: How quickly can a Midland County sale close?
faqs.a: With clean title and a current division order, most Midland County purchases close within two to four weeks. Interests needing probate or title curative work take longer, and we'll give you a realistic timeline upfront.

faqs.q: Why do you keep getting offer letters from different buyers for your Midland County interest?
faqs.a: Given how much documented activity and headquarters presence this county has, it draws more buyer competition than most surrounding counties. That's a reason to compare offers rather than accept the first one, and we're comfortable having our number reviewed against others.

faqs.q: Do you buy interests still tied to the original 1949 Spraberry discovery wells?
faqs.a: Yes, though most of those original wellbores have long since been replaced or supplemented by later development. We trace the full history from the original lease forward to whatever is currently producing on your tract.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Martin County, TX/NM
items.meta: Martin County sits in the core Midland Basin near Stanton, with some of the tightest well spacing in the Permian. We buy mineral and royalty interests here directly.

sections.html:
If you had to pick one county to explain why Wolfcamp horizontal drilling changed the Permian, you'd pick Martin County.

Martin County, with Stanton as the county seat, sits right in the middle of the Midland Basin's core acreage. Operators have run some of the tightest spacing units anywhere in the play here, stacking multiple Wolfcamp benches and the Spraberry above them under single drilling units. If you own minerals in Martin County, there's a good chance you're tied to a spacing unit that's seen more than one round of horizontal development since around 2012.

That density is good for royalty income but it also means the paperwork gets complicated fast. Division orders get amended as new wells come online, pooling orders stack, and it's not unusual for an owner to lose track of exactly how many wells they're actually in. We sort that out before we ever quote a number.

sections.title: Why this county draws aggressive development
sections.html:
The Wolfcamp interval under Martin County is thick and consistently productive across the county, without a lot of the geologic variability you see on the basin's edges. That consistency is exactly what makes it attractive to operators running full-scale development programs rather than single wildcat wells, they can plan a multi-year drilling program with confidence in the rock.

For mineral owners that's translated into repeated development on the same acreage over the last decade, sometimes three or four horizontal wells targeting different benches under one surface tract. It's also meant more competition among buyers for Martin County interests, which is worth knowing before you take the first offer that lands in your mailbox.

sections.title: How we price a Martin County interest
sections.html:
We pull your Railroad Commission lease and unit history first, looking at how many wellbores are actually producing against your tract, how recently they were completed, and where they sit on the decline curve. A unit with a well completed in the last two years prices very differently than one where every well was drilled a decade ago and is well into its tail production.

We also check adjacent sections for permits and rig activity. Operators here tend to develop in blocks, so activity next door is often a real signal about what's coming to your unit next rather than idle noise.

sections.title: Common ownership situations we see
sections.html:
A lot of Martin County minerals trace back to ranching families who held onto the mineral estate when land changed hands generations ago, so we regularly deal with fractional interests split among many heirs. We can buy one heir's share without requiring the whole family to agree.

We also see owners who leased years ago at a flat bonus and never expected the county to see this much development, and now hold a royalty interest worth more than they assumed. If that's you, we'll walk through exactly how the current production and nearby activity inform the number we offer.

faqs.q: Why does Martin County see so much repeat drilling on the same tracts?
faqs.a: The Wolfcamp interval here is thick and consistent, with multiple productive benches stacked under the Spraberry. That supports multi-well development programs where operators come back to the same units more than once as they target different zones.

faqs.q: How many wells might your interest actually be tied to?
faqs.a: It depends on your spacing unit, and it's common for owners to lose track after several rounds of development. We pull the full Railroad Commission history for your unit so you know exactly what's producing before we make an offer.

faqs.q: Is now a good time to sell in Martin County?
faqs.a: That depends on your goals and the specific activity near your tract. We'll show you what nearby permitting and completions look like so you can weigh selling now against holding for future development.

faqs.q: your family's interest is split among several heirs. Do you all have to sell together?
faqs.a: No. We can purchase one heir's fractional share on its own without the rest of the family agreeing to sell.

faqs.q: You leased years ago for a bonus payment. Is your royalty interest worth selling now?
faqs.a: Possibly, especially if there's been horizontal development since your lease was signed. We'll look at your actual production history and current royalty rate to tell you honestly what your interest is worth today.

faqs.q: Why do offers on Martin County minerals vary so much between buyers?
faqs.a: Different buyers use different assumptions about future drilling and decline rates, and some price off outdated production data. We build our number from your current division order and the actual Railroad Commission history for your unit, and we'll explain exactly how we got there.

faqs.q: Does Stanton's role as county seat affect how a sale is processed?
faqs.a: It mainly affects where title records are recorded and confirmed. The Martin County Clerk in Stanton holds the deeds, assignments, and probate filings we use to verify your ownership before closing.

faqs.q: What if you only own a small fraction of a spacing unit in Martin County?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are common here given how many owners a single unit can involve. We'll research and quote your specific share regardless of size, and you're free to sell independently of any co-owners.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Glasscock County, TX/NM
items.meta: Glasscock County is dead center in the Midland Basin's core. A retired operations engineer explains how royalty and mineral interests here get valued.

sections.html:
If you drew a bullseye on the Midland Basin, Glasscock County would sit close to the middle of it, and that geography shapes almost everything about how minerals here get priced.

Glasscock County has one of the lowest populations of any county in Texas, but per square mile it's one of the most heavily drilled counties in the entire Permian Basin. Garden City, the county seat, is barely a town, yet the Wolfcamp and Spraberry acreage surrounding it has supported some of the densest multi-well pad development we've seen in twenty-plus years around this business.

That combination, tiny population, massive drilling density, means a lot of mineral owners here inherited an interest from family land that's now sitting under some of the most competitively developed acreage in Texas without ever having set foot on it themselves. If that's you, we want to make sure you understand what your interest is actually worth before you decide anything.

sections.title: Small county, enormous drilling density
sections.html:
Glasscock County's population has stayed under two thousand for decades, but its permit counts and well density regularly rank among the top counties in the entire Permian Basin. Multiple large public operators run dense stacked-lateral programs across much of the county, targeting several Wolfcamp benches plus the Spraberry above them on the same sections.

That density is exactly why we treat Glasscock County minerals with a different level of attention than a comparably sized but lightly drilled county elsewhere in the basin. A single section here can carry a dozen or more producing horizontal wells across stacked zones, and your royalty decimal might touch several of them at once.

sections.title: Stacked-lateral development changes the math
sections.html:
When multiple operators are developing several benches on the same acreage, your royalty check can reflect production from wells landed at very different depths and drilled years apart, each on its own decline curve. That makes a simple 'multiply the current check by X' approach almost useless here, because the blended number hides what's actually happening well by well.

We pull the specific well history tied to your unit before we build an offer, looking at how many horizons are currently producing, how recently the newest ones came online, and whether there's still room for additional development on the same acreage. That's the difference between a real number and a guess.

sections.title: What actually sets value on your interest
sections.html:
Net royalty acres, current production across all producing horizons on your unit, overall decline trajectory, and remaining undrilled locations on the same acreage are the core inputs. Given how much of Glasscock County is already under active development, remaining undrilled locations often carry real weight rather than pure speculation, since the operators here have shown a consistent pattern of returning to fully develop acreage they've already permitted.

Values still vary with commodity pricing and the specific development stage of your unit, so we build a range off your actual documentation rather than quoting a flat number for the whole county.

sections.title: Ranch families and inherited fractions
sections.html:
Almost all of Glasscock County's private land traces back to a handful of large historic ranching families, and mineral ownership has fractionalized across generations the way it does everywhere land like this gets passed down. It's common for us to buy from an heir who holds a small decimal interest and has never lived anywhere near the county.

We're not a licensed appraiser, attorney, or CPA, and for questions about how a sale affects your estate or taxes, talk to your own advisor. What we offer is a direct look at your specific interest and a written offer with no pressure to accept it.

sections.title: What to send us first
sections.html:
A recent division order or check stub is the single most useful document, since it tells us the operator, the unit, and your decimal interest directly. If you're working from an old lease or a name in a probate file instead, that's still enough to start, and we'll cross-reference it against Texas Railroad Commission production records for the relevant sections.

We'll walk you through exactly how we arrived at any number we give you, well by well if that's what it takes, because given how many horizons can be producing under a single Glasscock County section, a vague explanation isn't good enough for either of us.

faqs.q: Why does Glasscock County have so much drilling for such a small population?
faqs.a: The county sits in the core of the Midland Basin with thick, stacked Wolfcamp and Spraberry pay, which supports dense multi-well pad development regardless of how few people live there. Well density and population aren't connected in a rural oilfield county like this one.

faqs.q: your royalty check seems to come from more than one well, is that normal here?
faqs.a: Very common. Stacked-lateral development means multiple horizons under the same acreage can be producing at once, sometimes drilled years apart. We break down the well-by-well history before valuing your interest rather than treating the blended check as one number.

faqs.q: Is there still room for new drilling on already-developed Glasscock County acreage?
faqs.a: Often yes. Operators here have consistently come back to fully develop acreage across multiple benches rather than drilling once and moving on, which is part of why undrilled locations on already-active units carry real weight in valuation.

faqs.q: You inherited a small fractional interest and never lived near Glasscock County, can you still help?
faqs.a: Yes, that's an extremely common situation here given how the land has passed through generations of a handful of ranching families. Send us your division order or check stub and we'll take it from there.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Howard County, TX/NM
items.meta: Own minerals in Howard County, Texas, near Big Spring? We buy Spraberry, San Andres and Wolfcamp interests directly and pay based on your real production and lease terms.

sections.html:
Howard County sits on the eastern hinge of the Midland Basin, where the same Spraberry and San Andres pay that made Midland famous starts to shallow out toward the Eastern Shelf.

We spent enough years running completions on the Midland side of the basin to know Howard County doesn't get talked about the way Martin or Midland County does, but the production history here is deep. Big Spring has been an oil town since the 1920s, and a lot of the minerals under this county were split up two and three generations ago, long before anyone was drilling laterals.

That history is exactly why owners here get confusing offers. Some of your acreage might be held by an old vertical San Andres well paying a few dollars a month, while a section line over a new Wolfcamp horizontal is running real volume. We look at both instead of whichever number makes an offer sound bigger.

sections.title: Where the county sits in the basin
sections.html:
The Midland Basin doesn't stop cleanly at a county line, and Howard County is proof. Moving east from Martin and Midland counties, the Spraberry and Wolfcamp intervals thin and the section starts to shelf out, which is why you'll see older, shallower San Andres and Clearfork wells mixed in with newer horizontal development. Big Spring, the county seat, grew up around that shallower production and the refinery that's operated there for decades.

For a mineral owner, that geologic transition matters more than it sounds. It means Howard County acreage can carry two very different production stories depending on exactly where your tract sits, and a buyer who only looks at a type curve for 'the Midland Basin' generally is going to miss it.

sections.title: What we actually price
sections.html:
When we look at a Howard County tract we're pulling your division order, your check stubs if you have them, and the Railroad Commission production history on the wellbore or unit you're tied to. If there's active horizontal development nearby with permits filed, that changes the offer. If your interest is under a decades-old vertical well on late-stage decline, that's a different conversation, and we'll tell you that up front rather than dress it up.

We also check for open acreage that hasn't been leased or held by production. Unleased minerals in a county with this much legacy vertical activity are common, and they get priced differently than a producing interest with a royalty history behind them.

sections.title: Heirship and fractional interests are common here
sections.html:
A meaningful share of the calls we get out of Howard County are from heirs splitting a tract that's been in the family since before the first oil boom. If you're one of six cousins each holding a small fractional interest in a producing well, that's a normal situation for us, not a complication. We can buy a single heir's share without requiring the rest of the family to sell.

If your interest hasn't been probated or the title has a gap somewhere, say a deed that never got recorded, we can usually still work with it, but it will affect timing. We'll walk you through what the courthouse records show before we ever put a number in front of you.

faqs.q: Is Howard County still seeing new drilling, or is it mostly legacy production?
faqs.a: Both. The western part of the county closer to Martin County sees ongoing horizontal Wolfcamp and Spraberry activity, while much of the rest of the county is older San Andres and Clearfork production on longer declines. We price your specific tract against the wells actually producing on or near it.

faqs.q: your family's minerals have been split between several heirs for decades. Can you still buy your share?
faqs.a: Yes. We buy individual fractional and undivided interests all the time and don't need the rest of your family to agree to sell alongside you.

faqs.q: What's a fair price for minerals near Big Spring?
faqs.a: It depends heavily on whether you're tied to active horizontal development or an older vertical well on decline, plus your net mineral acres and royalty rate. We quote against your actual production history rather than a flat countywide number.

faqs.q: Do you buy unleased minerals in Howard County?
faqs.a: We do, though the offer reflects that there's no royalty stream yet to underwrite it. Unleased acreage near confirmed horizontal permits is worth more than acreage with no nearby activity.

faqs.q: How fast can this close?
faqs.a: Once we've confirmed title through the county clerk's records and, if needed, probate documentation, most Howard County purchases close in three to six weeks. Clean title with a current division order moves faster.

faqs.q: Do you buy both mineral rights and royalty interests in Howard County?
faqs.a: Yes. A mineral owner who hasn't leased holds the right to lease and receive bonus and royalty, while a royalty owner is already receiving payments under an existing lease. We buy both, and the valuation approach differs between the two, so tell us which you have and we'll price it correctly.

faqs.q: What happens to your interest in the Big Spring refinery area if surface development expands?
faqs.a: Your mineral ownership stays separate from surface use under Texas law regardless of how the surface around Big Spring develops. We'll flag anything specific to your tract that could affect future drilling access, but the sale of your minerals isn't contingent on surface activity.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Ector County, TX/NM
items.meta: Ector County minerals sit near the busiest oilfield hub in the Permian. See how a retired operations engineer prices royalty and working interests here.

sections.html:
Odessa is the industry's front door to the Permian, and Ector County minerals underneath and around it get looked at differently than acreage further out.

Ector County is where a lot of the Permian's service and supply chain physically lives, but underneath that infrastructure sits some genuinely productive Wolfcamp and Spraberry acreage, plus a long tail of older vertical production going back generations. We've bought interests in both categories here, and the valuation approach for each is different enough that we want to walk through it plainly.

If you own a royalty or working interest in Ector County, whether it came to you through inheritance or you've held it for years, the county's mix of urban proximity, dense drilling history, and layered ownership makes it worth getting a real look at your specific tract rather than a generic county-wide estimate.

sections.title: Urban Odessa versus rural Ector County acreage
sections.html:
A meaningful share of Ector County's mineral estate sits under or near developed land around Odessa, which complicates drilling in ways that rural acreage in neighboring counties doesn't face. Setback requirements, surface use conflicts, and the practical difficulty of running a rig near residential or commercial development all factor into how operators plan around here.

Acreage further from the city, out toward Goldsmith and Gardendale, tends to see more straightforward horizontal development with fewer surface complications, and that generally shows up in how consistently those wells get drilled and produced. Neither situation makes an interest worthless, but it does change how we underwrite the risk.

sections.title: Decades of layered production history
sections.html:
Ector County has been producing oil since the 1920s, and a lot of the current mineral ownership traces back through several generations of the same families. That long history means we regularly see interests tied to old vertical Permian-age wells still producing modest volumes alongside newer horizontal Wolfcamp units on the same or adjacent tracts.

When both exist, your royalty check might be blending income from multiple wells with very different decline profiles, which is exactly the kind of situation where a generic online calculator gets it wrong. We pull the actual well history tied to your interest before we put a number in front of you.

sections.title: What actually sets the price
sections.html:
Net royalty acres, current production rate, decline stage, and nearby permitting activity are the core inputs, and they vary enough between a downtown-adjacent tract and a rural Ector County section that we won't quote a flat multiple for the whole county. What we can say honestly is that Ector County's dense operator activity and long production history tend to make title and production research more tractable than in newer, less-documented parts of the basin.

If your interest includes a working interest component rather than pure royalty, that changes the math meaningfully since you're on the hook for a share of operating costs. Tell us upfront which kind of interest you hold so the number we give you reflects your actual exposure.

sections.title: Working with heirs and split ownership
sections.html:
Because Ector County minerals have passed through generations of the same families, it's common for an interest to be split among a dozen or more heirs, sometimes with some shares undivided and unclear. We can typically buy your specific share without requiring the rest of the family to participate, and we've walked plenty of owners through exactly what documentation is needed to clear title on an inherited fractional interest.

None of this is legal or tax advice, and for probate or estate questions specific to your situation, talk to your attorney or CPA. What we bring is a straight cash offer built on real production data and no pressure to sign before you're ready.

sections.title: Timeline and what closing actually looks like
sections.html:
Once we agree on a number, we send a straightforward purchase and sale agreement, and our title work confirms your interest matches county and state records before anything closes. For most Ector County owners with clean title, that process runs three to six weeks from signature to funds in hand.

If there's an unresolved probate or a missing heir somewhere in the chain of title, that adds time, but it doesn't kill the deal. We've walked owners through exactly what curative steps are needed more than once, and we're happy to explain what your specific situation requires before you commit to anything.

faqs.q: Does it matter if your Ector County interest is near Odessa itself?
faqs.a: It can. Acreage close to developed parts of the city faces more surface-use and setback constraints on new drilling, which factors into value differently than open rural acreage further from town.

faqs.q: your check comes from an old vertical well, is that interest still worth selling?
faqs.a: Often yes, especially if there's newer horizontal development nearby or on the same tract. Even a modest, long-declining vertical well interest has value, and we evaluate it against actual production data rather than dismissing it.

faqs.q: You share ownership with several cousins you've never met, can you still buy your portion?

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Andrews County, TX/NM
items.meta: Own minerals or royalty in Andrews County? A former operations engineer explains what drives value there and how a fair cash offer actually gets built.

sections.html:
Andrews County sits on the western shelf of the Midland Basin, and we've spent enough years looking at logs from this county to know it rewards patience more than headlines.

We ran drilling and completions programs in the Midland Basin for the better part of two decades before we started buying royalty interests full time, and Andrews County was always one of the counties where the Wolfcamp and Spraberry sections behaved consistently enough that operators could plan multi-well pads years out. That consistency is exactly why an interest here tends to hold value even when a single well's decline curve looks rough on paper.

If you inherited a fractional royalty interest, or you're the owner of record on a lease that's been producing since a relative signed it decades ago, here is what actually moves the number on an offer for Andrews County minerals, and what we'd want to know before we put a figure in front of you.

sections.title: Where the county sits in the play
sections.html:
Andrews County straddles the northwestern edge of the Midland Basin, with the county seat of Andrews serving as the hub for the oilfield service traffic that runs between here and the New Mexico state line. The Wolfcamp A and B benches carry most of the current horizontal activity, stacked above older vertical Spraberry and San Andres production that in some sections has been running since the 1950s.

What that layered history means for a mineral owner is that your interest may be earning off more than one producing horizon, or it may sit under acreage that's been held by production for so long the original lease terms are almost antique. Both situations change how we'd approach valuing the interest, which is why we always ask for the lease number or at least the operator name before quoting anything.

sections.title: What drives the number on an offer
sections.html:
Three things move a valuation more than anything else: net royalty acres, the decline stage of the wells currently paying you, and whether there's undeveloped acreage nearby that a public operator has already permitted. In parts of Andrews County near the more active pad development, that third factor can matter as much as your current check amount, because a buyer is pricing in wells that haven't spud yet.

Values here vary with commodity price, spacing, and where exactly your tract sits relative to the current drilling program, so we won't quote a multiple without seeing the tract. What we can tell you is that a royalty statement showing steady or gently declining production from a recent Wolfcamp horizontal is generally viewed differently than one showing a legacy vertical well thirty years into its life. Both still have value, they're just priced against different assumptions.

sections.title: Ownership situations we see most in Andrews County
sections.html:
A lot of the mineral ownership here traces back to ranching families who held onto minerals when they sold or leased surface acreage generations ago, so it's common to find an interest split five or six ways among heirs who've never met each other. If you're one of several siblings or cousins holding a fractional piece, we can usually work with your share alone without requiring everyone else to sell.

We also see non-operated working interests in Andrews County, usually held by someone who was cut into a deal decades ago or inherited a small working interest alongside the royalty. Working interest carries cost exposure that royalty doesn't, and that changes the math meaningfully, so tell us upfront which kind of interest you hold.

sections.title: What we need to put a real number in front of you
sections.html:
A recent division order or royalty check stub gets us most of the way there. The operator name, the well or unit name, and your decimal interest let us pull production history from state records and build an honest range instead of a guess. If you don't have paperwork handy, the county and roughly where the tract sits is enough to start.

We're not a licensed appraiser and this isn't a substitute for legal or tax advice on your specific situation, so for anything involving estate division or the tax treatment of a sale, talk to your CPA or attorney before you sign. What we can do is give you a candid, no-pressure number based on how we'd actually price the interest if we were buying it ourselves, because we am.

faqs.q: Do you need to know which wells are producing on your Andrews County interest before contacting you?
faqs.a: No. If you have a recent check stub or division order, that's plenty. If you don't, we can often locate the unit using your legal description or the operator's name and cross-reference it against Texas Railroad Commission records.

faqs.q: Does it matter if your Andrews County minerals are held by production or sitting undeveloped?
faqs.a: It matters for pricing but not for whether we can make an offer. Producing interests are valued off current cash flow and decline behavior. Undeveloped or non-producing acreage is valued more on nearby permitting activity and how likely a well is to be drilled in a reasonable window.

faqs.q: You only own a small fractional interest, is it worth selling?
faqs.a: Small fractional interests are exactly what we buy most often in this county, since so much of the original mineral estate has been divided among heirs. A tiny decimal interest is still real money if the underlying wells are productive.

faqs.q: How fast can a sale close on an Andrews County royalty interest?
faqs.a: Once we have a signed purchase and sale agreement and title work confirms your interest, most closings run three to six weeks. Title curative issues, like unresolved probate on an inherited interest, can extend that timeline.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Reagan County, TX/NM
items.meta: Reagan County minerals near Big Lake, where the Permian Basin was discovered in 1923, can be worth more than owners realize. Get a candid, no-pressure valuation.

sections.html:
Reagan County is where the Permian Basin got its start in 1923, and 100 years later it's still one of the more consistently drilled parts of the Midland side of the play.

Every geology class we ever sat through mentioned Santa Rita No. 1 — the well that blew in southwest of Big Lake and told the world there was oil under all this ranchland. That history matters for more than trivia; it means Reagan County has more decades of continuous drilling, more legacy leases, and more layered title than almost anywhere else on the Midland side of the basin.

It also means a good chunk of the county's minerals sit under University Lands acreage — the Permanent University Fund tracts that stretch across several counties here — which changes the leasing and development picture on adjacent private minerals. If you own a fractional interest near Big Lake or out toward the county lines, we'll tell you plainly whether you're next to that University Lands activity or sitting on something quieter.

sections.title: Big Lake and a century of Spraberry production
sections.html:
Big Lake is the county seat and sits close to where it all started. The Spraberry Trend covers most of the county, and while the original vertical wells from the mid-20th century have mostly declined to stripper-well volumes, the same rock has been redrilled horizontally over the last 15 years with far better recovery. That means it's not unusual to find a family whose grandparents leased this ground in the 1950s now watching a brand-new horizontal well go in on the same section.

That layering — old vertical held-by-production leases sitting under newer horizontal development — is one of the more common title situations we run into in Reagan County, and it's exactly the kind of thing that needs a careful read before anyone quotes you a number.

sections.title: University Lands as a neighbor, not necessarily your owner
sections.html:
A lot of people hear 'University Lands' and assume it means the state owns everything out here. It doesn't — University Lands controls specific tracts under the Permanent University Fund, and plenty of private mineral ownership sits right alongside it, often on the same section or adjacent ones. What matters for you is that operators drilling university acreage frequently hold leases on the neighboring private minerals too, which tends to keep private tracts in Reagan County in the development conversation rather than forgotten.

If your family's minerals border University Lands acreage, that's usually a good sign for activity level, even if the university tract itself gets more press.

sections.title: Spacing units and why one lease can cover a lot of family
sections.html:
Modern horizontal spacing units in Reagan County commonly run a mile or more, pooling multiple original tracts and, often, multiple original mineral owners into a single unit. If your family's original allotment was 160 or 320 acres, there's a decent chance it's now part of a much larger unit alongside neighbors you've never met, all sharing production from wells that may not even sit on your specific acres.

That's normal under Texas pooling and doesn't reduce your ownership — you're paid your proportionate share regardless of where the wellbore physically sits — but it does mean your royalty statement can look confusing if you're not used to reading unit decimal interests. We're glad to walk through yours line by line before you decide anything.

sections.title: What clean and messy title look like here
sections.html:
Because so much of this county's mineral ownership dates back to the original ranching families and early-1900s land patents, clean title is the exception more than the rule. Multiple generations of heirs, undivided interests split six or eight ways, and the occasional missing probate record are common. The county clerk in Big Lake holds the records, and a competent landman can usually reconstruct a chain even when your own paperwork is thin.

None of that should stop you from asking what your interest is worth. Bring what you have — a division order, an old lease, even just a royalty check stub with an owner number on it — and we'll figure out the rest from the courthouse records.

faqs.q: Is Reagan County still an active area for new drilling, or is it mostly old wells?
faqs.a: Both. There's a long tail of legacy vertical Spraberry production, but the same formations have been actively redrilled horizontally over the past decade, particularly on and near University Lands acreage. We check current permitting on your specific section rather than assuming based on the county's age as a producing area.

faqs.q: your mineral interest borders University Lands. Does that affect its value?
faqs.a: It can help. Operators developing University Lands tracts often hold leases on adjoining private minerals, which tends to keep those private interests in active development plans rather than sitting idle. We look at what's happening on and around your specific tract before quoting a number.

faqs.q: Why is your royalty check from a Reagan County well smaller than you expected given how big the unit is?
faqs.a: Modern spacing units often pool a mile or more of acreage across many original owners, so your check reflects your proportionate decimal interest in the unit, not the whole well's production. We can walk through your division order and explain exactly how your share was calculated.

faqs.q: What if you only have a fraction of a fraction — is it even worth selling?
faqs.a: Often yes. Small fractional interests are common in Reagan County given how many generations of heirs some tracts have passed through, and buyers regularly purchase these smaller pieces. It's usually more trouble to keep tracking a tiny scattered interest than to convert it to a lump sum.

faqs.q: How do you value a Reagan County interest that's next to a working University Lands rig but not on it?
faqs.a: We look at the unit your tract is actually pooled into, the wells producing from that unit, decline history, and current activity nearby, rather than proximity to a rig you can see from the road. Two adjacent tracts can carry very different values depending on which unit each is pooled into.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Upton County, TX/NM
items.meta: Own minerals in Upton County near Rankin or McCamey? Get a plain-spoken valuation from someone who reads the Spraberry decline curves, not a form-letter offer.

sections.html:
Upton County is quieter than its Midland and Ector neighbors, but the Spraberry Trend runs through it just the same, and the ranching families who've held minerals here for generations often have no idea what a fair number looks like today.

Rankin, the county seat, is a small enough town that everybody knows whose cattle are whose, and a lot of the mineral ownership out here traces back the same way — original ranching-family allotments, split among children and grandchildren, some of whom left West Texas decades ago and haven't thought about the mineral deed since. McCamey, over toward the county's western edge, has its own long oilfield history going back to the 1920s boom.

What's changed in the last several years is that horizontal Spraberry and Wolfcamp development, which built out heavily in neighboring Midland and Reagan counties, has continued to push into Upton County acreage. If your family's minerals have sat quiet for a long time, it's worth checking whether that's still true before assuming the interest isn't worth much.

sections.title: Rankin, McCamey, and a county built on ranching and oil together
sections.html:
Upton County has never had a large population, and that's kept a lot of its mineral ownership concentrated in the same handful of original ranching families rather than scattered through corporate turnover the way some other Permian counties have. That can be an advantage for owners — records tend to be more traceable when the same names have held the ground for generations — but it also means a lot of interests here are small undivided fractions split among a wide circle of heirs.

McCamey's oil history predates most of the current horizontal boom by nearly a century, and some of the older vertical production out that way is still paying modest, steady checks even now.

sections.title: Riding the edge of the Spraberry core
sections.html:
Upton County sits along the southern and western edge of the dense Spraberry and Wolfcamp development that's concentrated more heavily in Midland and Martin counties to the north. That edge position means activity here can be more selective — good acreage gets drilled aggressively, while other parts of the county see far less attention.

That's exactly why a fair valuation on an Upton County interest has to start with checking current permits and nearby unit activity on your specific section, not a general sense of how busy the Permian is right now. Two tracts a few miles apart can have very different outlooks.

sections.title: Small fractional interests are the norm here, not the exception
sections.html:
Because so much of the county's minerals trace back to a handful of original ranching allotments now split among generations of heirs, it's common to run into owners with interests measured in tiny decimals — a 1/64th here, a 1/256th there. These are easy to lose track of and easy to undervalue, since the checks, when they come, are small enough that many owners never bother finding out what the underlying interest itself is worth.

We buy interests of any size. A small fractional interest that's been sitting forgotten in a filing cabinet can still add up to a meaningful lump sum, especially if it sits under acreage that's seeing renewed development.

sections.title: Getting title straight through the Rankin courthouse
sections.html:
The Upton County clerk's office in Rankin holds records that, for the older ranching-family tracts, can run back the better part of a century. Probate gaps are common where an owner passed without a will, or where heirs never formally recorded their inherited share. None of that is unusual for this county and none of it should discourage you from asking what your interest is worth.

Bring whatever you have, even a decades-old lease or a single check stub, and we'll do the courthouse work to confirm the chain of title before closing.

faqs.q: your family's Upton County minerals haven't paid anything in years. Are they worth selling?
faqs.a: Sometimes, yes, if there's renewed drilling activity nearby, since a currently non-producing interest can still hold significant value based on future potential. We check current permitting near your specific tract before telling you whether it's worth pursuing.

faqs.q: You only own a small fractional interest, like a 64th or smaller. Do you buy those?
faqs.a: Yes. Small fractional interests are common in Upton County given how many generations some ranching-family tracts have passed through, and we regularly purchase interests of any size.

faqs.q: Is Upton County actively being drilled right now?
faqs.a: It sits on the edge of the dense Spraberry and Wolfcamp core to the north, so activity varies more by specific tract than in counties like Martin or Midland. We look at permits and unit activity near your acreage specifically rather than the county as a whole.

faqs.q: your paperwork on this interest is old and incomplete. What do you do?
faqs.a: Bring what you have — an old lease, a check stub, anything with an owner or well name on it. We use that as a starting point and confirm the rest through Upton County clerk records in Rankin before closing.

faqs.q: Can you sell just your Upton County interest and keep minerals you own elsewhere?
faqs.a: Yes. We price and close on individual tracts or interests, so you can sell one property while holding onto others in different counties or states.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Ward County, TX/NM
items.meta: Ward County minerals near Monahans span decades-old vertical wells and new Delaware Basin horizontals. Get a valuation that accounts for both.

sections.html:
Ward County, home to Monahans, has some of the oldest continuously producing acreage in the Permian sitting right alongside newer horizontal development, and knowing which one your family's minerals fall under changes everything about what they're worth.

Monahans has been an oil town since long before the Delaware Basin horizontal boom, and Ward County carries that history in its title records — leases from the 1930s and 1940s, held by production for decades on shallow vertical wells that still pump a few barrels a day. That's one layer of ownership here.

The other layer is newer: Wolfcamp horizontal development pushing in from the more active parts of the Delaware Basin to the south and west, picking up acreage that had been quiet for years. If your family's minerals sit in Ward County, we'll tell you plainly which layer you're in — and whether recent permitting has changed the picture on ground that used to be considered tapped out.

sections.title: Monahans and the county's deep production history
sections.html:
Monahans sits close to some of the earliest developed acreage in this part of the Permian, and a lot of Ward County's mineral title reflects that — leases that have been held by production continuously since well before most current owners were born. Those older vertical wells produce modestly now, but the leases themselves are often still active, which matters if a new operator wants to redrill the same acreage horizontally.

The Monahans Sandhills, the dune field the town is named near, sits over part of this legacy production and remains largely undeveloped surface even where the minerals below have been leased and drilled for generations.

sections.title: Where new Delaware Basin horizontals are reaching into Ward County
sections.html:
Operators active in the busier parts of the Delaware Basin to the south, around Reeves and Loving counties, have steadily extended horizontal development north and east into parts of Ward County. That's changed the calculus for owners whose minerals sat under old, low-producing vertical wells for decades — some of that acreage is now getting a second look for horizontal Wolfcamp development.

If you haven't checked on your Ward County interest in a while, it's worth confirming whether any new permits have gone in nearby before assuming nothing's changed.

sections.title: Old leases, new operators
sections.html:
It's common in Ward County to find a mineral deed and lease from decades ago still technically controlling the acreage, even though the operator currently producing it isn't the same company that signed the original lease. Leases and working interests here have changed hands many times over the decades through mergers, sales, and assignments, and your division order should reflect whoever's currently paying — but the underlying lease terms can still trace back to a document your grandparents signed.

That layered history is normal for a county this old in oil terms, and it's exactly the kind of thing a careful title review sorts out before anyone quotes you a fair number.

sections.title: Courthouse records in Monahans
sections.html:
The Ward County clerk's office holds records stretching back nearly a century in places, which is both a blessing and a challenge — deep history means more documentation to work through, but also more opportunity for gaps: unrecorded assignments, probate that never got filed, name changes across generations. None of that is unusual here.

Bring whatever you have, even something as old as an original 1940s lease, and we'll do the work of tracing it forward to confirm current ownership before closing.

faqs.q: your family's Ward County lease is from the 1940s. Is it still valid?
faqs.a: Often, yes, if it's been continuously held by production, which is common in this county. Old leases don't expire just because they're old, as long as production has continued without a lapse. We verify this through Ward County clerk records before valuing your interest.

faqs.q: Is Ward County seeing any new drilling, or is it all old wells?
faqs.a: Both. There's deep legacy vertical production around Monahans, and newer Wolfcamp horizontal development has been extending in from the more active Delaware Basin counties to the south. We check current permits near your specific tract rather than assuming based on the county's older reputation.

faqs.q: The operator on your check isn't the company your grandparents originally leased to. Is that a problem?
faqs.a: No, that's normal. Leases and operating interests in Ward County have changed hands many times over the decades. As long as your division order reflects the current operator and your interest is accurately calculated, the change of hands doesn't affect your ownership.

faqs.q: How does the Monahans Sandhills area affect drilling or mineral value nearby?
faqs.a: The dune field itself is mostly undeveloped surface, but the minerals beneath and around it have been leased and produced for decades. Surface terrain doesn't typically limit horizontal drilling the way it might have limited older vertical operations, so nearby acreage remains in play.

faqs.q: What does closing look like for an older Ward County lease with limited paperwork?
faqs.a: We start with whatever documents you have and use Ward County clerk records in Monahans to trace the chain of title forward from there. Older leases with gaps take a bit more time to clear, but we handle that work and keep you informed rather than asking you to track it down yourself.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Winkler County, TX/NM
items.meta: Winkler County minerals sit over the historic Hendrick Field and newer Delaware Basin horizontals near Kermit and Wink. Get a valuation that separates the two.

sections.html:
Winkler County has been producing oil since 1926, and between the Hendrick Field's long secondary-recovery life and newer horizontal drilling to the south, few counties in the Permian carry more layered mineral history per square mile.

Kermit is the county seat, and Wink sits close enough that the two towns share a lot of the same oilfield story. Hendrick Field, discovered in 1926, was for a long time one of the largest oil fields in the Permian Basin, and it's still producing today through decades of waterflood and enhanced recovery on wells that were drilled when your great-grandparents were young.

Winkler County is also home to two well-documented sinkholes near Wink, formed by decades of old wellbore casing failures interacting with the Salado salt formation below — a real geological fact locally, and something owners sometimes ask about, though it has no bearing on mineral ownership or value elsewhere in the county. What matters more for most owners here is whether their acreage sits in the mature Hendrick Field footprint or in the newer horizontal Delaware Basin acreage further south.

sections.title: Newer Delaware Basin horizontal development to the south
sections.html:
South of the historic field, Winkler County acreage overlaps with the newer horizontal Wolfcamp development that's built out heavily in neighboring Ward and Loving counties. Operators have extended horizontal units into southern Winkler County acreage over the past several years, and that acreage behaves very differently than the mature Hendrick Field ground — higher initial production, steeper decline curves, and generally stronger current interest from buyers.

Knowing which part of the county your tract falls in changes the valuation conversation substantially, which is why we check current permits and unit activity on your specific section before quoting anything.

sections.title: Hendrick Field and nearly a century of continuous production
sections.html:
Hendrick Field has been under some form of active operation almost continuously since the 1920s, moving from primary production through waterflood and other secondary recovery methods over the decades. That kind of longevity means leases here have been held by production for generations, and mineral ownership has often passed through several rounds of inheritance without ever lapsing.

Checks from Hendrick Field acreage today tend to be modest and steady, reflecting mature secondary-recovery production rather than a new well's initial output. For owners with small fractional interests here, that steady but limited monthly income is often the whole reason to consider a sale — converting decades of small checks into one number now.

sections.title: Title through generations in Kermit
sections.html:
The Winkler County clerk's office in Kermit holds records reflecting a century of nearly continuous oil activity, which means deep documentation but also, for many family tracts, deep complexity — interests split among heirs across four or five generations, old assignments between long-since-merged companies, and the occasional gap that takes courthouse work to fill.

None of that should discourage you from finding out what your interest is worth. Bring whatever paperwork you have, and we'll do the work to confirm the chain of title before closing.

sections.title: The Wink sinkholes, and why they don't change your mineral value
sections.html:
The two sinkholes near Wink are a real, documented local phenomenon tied to old, deteriorated wellbore casings interacting with the underlying salt formation, and they've drawn genuine geological study over the years. They're isolated to specific tracts near those old wellbores, not a county-wide issue, and they don't affect mineral ownership, title, or the value of interests elsewhere in Winkler County.

If you've heard about the sinkholes and wondered whether they say something about the safety or value of your own interest, the honest answer is almost certainly no unless your specific tract sits on one of the affected sites.

faqs.q: Is your Winkler County interest tied to the old Hendrick Field, or newer drilling?
faqs.a: It depends on exactly where your tract sits. Hendrick Field production, mostly north and central in the county, is mature secondary-recovery output. Newer horizontal Wolfcamp development has extended into acreage further south. We check your specific section before telling you which situation applies.

faqs.q: Do the sinkholes near Wink affect the value of mineral rights elsewhere in the county?
faqs.a: No. The sinkholes are tied to specific deteriorated old wellbores near Wink and are a localized, well-documented geological issue, not a county-wide condition. They don't affect title or value on tracts elsewhere in Winkler County.

faqs.q: your checks from a Hendrick Field well are small and have been for years. Is your interest still worth anything?
faqs.a: Often, yes, even at modest monthly income, since the underlying interest carries value beyond the current check size, particularly given the near century of continuous production history behind it. We factor in the full production history rather than the most recent statement alone.

faqs.q: How do you know if your Winkler County minerals are near any new drilling?
faqs.a: We check current state permitting near your specific tract as part of any valuation, so you'll know honestly whether there's recent or planned activity nearby before you decide anything.

faqs.q: Can you handle a Winkler County interest that's been split among a lot of heirs over the generations?
faqs.a: Yes. Given the county's century-long production history, multi-generation heirship is common. We work with a title company to trace ownership through Winkler County clerk records in Kermit and can typically purchase just your undivided share without requiring every heir to participate.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Reeves County, TX/NM
items.meta: Reeves County sits in the busiest part of the Delaware Basin. If you own minerals or royalty near Pecos or Toyah, get a real number based on current activity.

sections.html:
Reeves County, with Pecos as the county seat, is about as active as Permian drilling gets right now, and that activity is exactly what's pushing offers on private minerals here higher than in quieter counties.

We've driven the roads around Pecos and Toyah enough times to lose count of the frac spreads, water lines, and man-camp trailers that have gone up in the last several years. This is stacked-pay country — Wolfcamp, Bone Spring, and Avalon shale all producing from the same general acreage, sometimes from the same multi-well pad drilled to different depths. That kind of density is exactly why Reeves County minerals tend to command real attention from buyers.

But density also means complexity. A single section here might have three or four operators with overlapping units at different depths, produced water recycling infrastructure crossing the surface, and permits stacking up faster than most owners can track on their own. If you've got a royalty check coming out of Reeves County, or a mineral deed your family's held since before any of this started, we'll walk you through exactly what's producing under your acres before quoting anything.

sections.title: Pecos, Toyah, and the busiest stretch of the Delaware Basin
sections.html:
Pecos sits close to the center of the most heavily drilled part of the Delaware Basin, and the pace of permitting here over the last decade has been hard to match anywhere else in the play. Toyah, a little east along the old Texas and Pacific rail line, sits in similarly active acreage. If your family's minerals are anywhere in this corridor, there's a good chance multiple operators have looked at your section even if only one currently holds the lease.

That density cuts both ways for owners. It generally means stronger current activity and more competitive leasing, but it also means more overlapping paperwork — separate units for separate formations stacked on the same surface acres — which takes a careful hand to untangle before anyone can tell you what your specific interest is worth.

sections.title: Stacked benches mean stacked units
sections.html:
Because Reeves County produces from multiple formations at different depths under the same acreage, it's common for your minerals to be pooled into more than one spacing unit simultaneously — one for a Wolfcamp bench, another for Bone Spring, sometimes a third. Each unit can have a different operator, different working interest partners, and a different decline curve.

That means a Reeves County owner might get two or three separate royalty checks off the same tract, each behaving differently. It's one of the more common sources of confusion we run into with owners here, and it's also why a fair valuation has to account for every unit your acreage touches, rather than only the one you happen to have a check for.

sections.title: Water, infrastructure, and what it means for your minerals
sections.html:
The scale of drilling in Reeves County has driven massive investment in produced water recycling and disposal infrastructure — pipelines, recycling facilities, and salt water disposal wells that crisscross the county alongside the oil and gas wells themselves. None of that changes your mineral ownership directly, but it's a reasonable proxy for how committed operators are to this acreage long-term: nobody builds permanent water infrastructure on ground they plan to walk away from soon.

For owners deciding whether to hold or sell, that long-term operator commitment is worth factoring in. It generally supports continued development rather than a quick boom-and-bust.

sections.title: Title work through the Reeves County clerk's office
sections.html:
Reeves County has seen enough oil-driven land transactions over the past century that courthouse records in Pecos can run deep and, in places, messy — assignments from decades ago, name variations across generations, and fractional interests split among heirs who've since moved away from West Texas entirely. A buyer working in good faith runs full title before closing regardless of what paperwork you personally have on hand.

If you've got a division order number, an old lease, or even just a check stub, that's enough to start. We do the courthouse work from there and tell you honestly if anything needs to be cleared before we can close.

faqs.q: Why does your Reeves County royalty check come from a different operator than the one you originally leased with?
faqs.a: Leases and operating rights change hands frequently in an active area like this. Operators buy, sell, and swap acreage regularly, and your division order should reflect the current operator. If your paperwork looks outdated, we can help track down who's currently paying and what unit you're in.

faqs.q: You get two separate royalty checks for what you thought was one piece of land. Is that normal?
faqs.a: Very common in Reeves County. Because multiple formations are developed at different depths under the same surface acreage, your minerals can be pooled into separate units for each bench, each paying its own royalty. We account for every unit your tract touches when we value your interest.

faqs.q: Is Reeves County still seeing new wells, or has development slowed?
faqs.a: It remains one of the more actively permitted counties in the Delaware Basin. That said, activity varies block by block, so we check current permitting near your specific unit rather than assuming based on the county's overall reputation.

faqs.q: Does the water recycling and pipeline infrastructure on the surface affect your mineral value?
faqs.a: Not directly — that's surface infrastructure and doesn't change your mineral ownership. But it's a reasonable signal that operators are committed to developing this acreage for the long haul, which we factor into how we think about future activity on your tract.

faqs.q: How fast can you close on a Reeves County mineral sale?
faqs.a: With clean, traceable title we can often close in two to four weeks. Given how much land here has changed hands over the decades, some tracts need extra title work first — we'll tell you honestly which situation yours is before you sign anything.
