items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Loving County, TX/NM
items.meta: Loving County has under a hundred residents but sits on some of the densest horizontal drilling in the Delaware Basin. We buy minerals here directly, no listing required.

sections.html:
Loving County is the least populated county in the United States and one of the most heavily drilled square miles in the entire Permian Basin, which makes it a strange place to own minerals.

We've worked acreage all over the Delaware Basin and Loving County still stands out. There are more producing wellbores here than there are people, and most owners with an interest in this county don't live anywhere near Mentone, the county seat. A lot of these tracts trace back to ranching families who never expected the ground under their cattle to sit over some of the most active Wolfcamp and Bone Spring horizontal development in Texas.

Because so few people actually live on the surface here, mineral records can be thin on local knowledge, courthouse staff turnover is high, and title work sometimes takes patience. That's exactly the kind of situation we're set up to handle without slowing you down more than necessary.

sections.title: Core Delaware Basin geology, no shelf to hide behind
sections.html:
Unlike a county like Lea or Eddy where you're dealing with a shelf side and a basin side, Loving County sits almost entirely in the deep, core Delaware Basin. That means stacked Wolfcamp and Bone Spring benches, thick Delaware sand intervals, and operators running multi-well pads that can hold six, eight, or more laterals under a single surface location. Well density here is about as high as anywhere in the Permian.

For an owner, that generally means more wells touching your acreage over time, which can mean more royalty checks, but it also means more spacing unit paperwork, more pooling orders, and more division order amendments to track. We check every unit your interest could be tied to rather than only the well you're currently getting paid on.

sections.title: Why offers here move fast
sections.html:
With this much active permitting and drilling concentrated in one county, operators are often working several sections at once, and new permits can shift the value of a tract quickly. If we see a permit filed on an offset unit to your acreage, that changes our number, sometimes within weeks of the filing showing up.

That cuts both ways for a seller. If you're hoping a new well gets drilled near your tract before you sell, that can raise the price. If you'd rather lock in value now rather than wait through years of drilling and decline, that's a reasonable call too, and it's yours to make. We'll tell you honestly what nearby permitting suggests either way.

sections.title: Out-of-state and multi-generation ownership
sections.html:
Given how few people actually live in Loving County, most of the mineral owners we talk to here are elsewhere, often several states away, holding an interest that came down through a ranching family or an old land trade. We handle closing entirely by mail and wire, you don't need to be anywhere near Mentone to sell.

If your interest was split among siblings or cousins decades ago and nobody's kept it organized since, we're used to piecing that together from the county clerk's real property records and Railroad Commission unit filings.

faqs.q: Loving County has almost no residents. How do you handle title work with so little local infrastructure?
faqs.a: We pull directly from the county clerk's recorded instruments and Railroad Commission filings rather than relying on local knowledge. It can take a bit longer than a county with more staff, but it's routine for us.

faqs.q: Why is Loving County drilled so densely?
faqs.a: It sits in the core of the Delaware Basin with thick, stacked Wolfcamp and Bone Spring pay, which supports multi-well pads with several laterals under one surface location. Well density here is among the highest in the Permian.

faqs.q: Should you wait to sell until a new well is permitted near your tract?
faqs.a: It depends on your goals. New permitting nearby can raise value, but it's not guaranteed and can take years to produce a check. We'll give you an honest read on nearby activity so you can decide what fits your situation.

faqs.q: You don't live in Texas and have never been to Mentone. Can you still sell?
faqs.a: Yes, and most of our Loving County sellers are in the same position. Closing happens by mail and wire transfer, no travel required.

faqs.q: How is a working interest in Loving County different to sell than a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A working interest owner shares in drilling and operating costs, so we price it against net proceeds after those costs rather than gross royalty. Let us know which type of interest you hold and we'll quote it correctly the first time.

faqs.q: How do pooling orders affect a Loving County sale?
faqs.a: With this much multi-well pad development, your acreage is often pooled into more than one spacing unit across different Wolfcamp and Bone Spring benches. We review every pooling order tied to your tract so the offer reflects everything you're actually entitled to, instead of only the most recent order you may have on file.

faqs.q: Can you close before the end of the year for tax planning purposes?
faqs.a: We can move quickly once title is confirmed, but exact timing depends on your specific documentation. Let us know your target date early and we'll tell you honestly whether it's realistic for your interest.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Pecos County, TX/NM
items.meta: Own minerals or royalty in Pecos County, TX? Get a straight, no-obligation look at what your Delaware Basin interest is worth today.

sections.html:
Pecos County runs from the ranch country south of Fort Stockton into some of the most drilled acreage on the western Delaware shelf, and what your interest is worth depends entirely on which side of the county line you're standing on.

We spent enough years on drilling rigs west of Fort Stockton to know Pecos County doesn't behave like one basin. The western half is still mostly Ellenburger and Devonian vertical production, some of it dating back to the 1950s, held by families who've cashed the same small check every month for two generations. The eastern half, up against the Reeves County line, is a different animal entirely — stacked Wolfcamp and Bone Spring benches, multi-well horizontal pads, and operators who weren't drilling there ten years ago.

If you inherited a fraction here, or your grandfather leased 640 acres south of we-10 back when Fort Stockton was still mostly sheep and cattle, the fair value of that interest hinges on whether you're sitting under active development or legacy vertical wells that peaked decades ago. We look at both the same way — pull the runsheet, check who's operating nearby, and tell you honestly which bucket you're in before we quote a number.

sections.title: What a royalty check from Pecos County actually looks like
sections.html:
If you're getting a statement from an operator on eastern Pecos County acreage, expect it to move — sometimes sharply — with new wells coming online in the unit, then decline steadily as those wells mature. That volatility is exactly why some owners choose to sell: locking in a value now avoids riding the decline curve down over the next several years, especially if you don't need the monthly income and would rather have the lump sum.

On the western, older-vertical side of the county, checks tend to be smaller and steadier, and a sale there is usually less about timing the market and more about simplifying an estate or converting a tiny, easy-to-lose-track-of interest into cash you can actually use.

sections.title: Fort Stockton, Sheffield, and the county's two personalities
sections.html:
Fort Stockton is the county seat and where you'll find the courthouse records, but it's also roughly the dividing line for the geology that matters to your check. West and south of town, toward the Glass Mountains and the Trans-Pecos ranch country, most of the production is older, shallower, and declining the way you'd expect a 40-year-old vertical well to decline — slow, low-volume, predictable.

East toward Sheffield and the Reeves County boundary, Apache and other operators have been running horizontal Wolfcamp and Bone Spring laterals through stacked pay for the better part of a decade. That's the part of the county where a small legacy interest can suddenly be worth multiples of what it was five years ago, simply because a new unit got permitted across it. Knowing which side of that line your tract sits on is the first thing we check, not the last.

sections.title: University and state land neighbors
sections.html:
Pecos County sits close enough to University Lands' Permian holdings that a lot of the operators active on private minerals here are the same names running rigs on state and university acreage a county or two over. That matters because it means the drilling pace on your section can be driven by an operator's broader development plan rather than anything specific to your tract — a good reason to check current permitting before assuming your interest is dormant just because nothing's happened on it in a while.

It also means split estate is common. A lot of the ranching families out here sold the surface generations ago but kept the minerals, or the reverse, and title can carry surface-use agreements, old pooling orders, or non-participating royalty carve-outs that a buyer needs to read carefully before quoting anything.

sections.title: Working from a Pecos County courthouse title
sections.html:
The county clerk's office in Fort Stockton holds deed and probate records going back to the county's earliest oil days, and because so much of this land changed hands through ranching-family inheritance rather than clean corporate sale, a lot of the mineral title out here runs through wills, heirship affidavits, and undivided fractional interests split among cousins who may not all agree on what to do.

That's normal, not a dealbreaker. We've bought fractional interests where four heirs wanted to sell and one didn't — you can typically sell just your undivided share without forcing anyone else's hand. Bring whatever paperwork you have, even if it's incomplete; a probate gap or an old unrecorded assignment doesn't kill a deal, it just means the closing takes a little longer while title gets cleared.

faqs.q: Does it matter whether your Pecos County minerals are on the east or west side of the county?
faqs.a: Yes, considerably. Eastern acreage near the Reeves County line sits under active Wolfcamp and Bone Spring horizontal development, which tends to support a higher valuation than older vertical production farther west and south. We check current permitting near your specific tract before quoting anything, rather than pricing off a county-wide average.

faqs.q: your family has owned this interest since before you was born and the paperwork is thin. Can you still buy it?
faqs.a: Usually, yes. Pecos County has a long history of minerals passing through ranching-family inheritance, so incomplete records are common, not unusual. We work with a title company to fill gaps using probate and heirship records at the courthouse in Fort Stockton, and that process rarely stops a sale — it just adds time.

faqs.q: Is your royalty check from Pecos County likely to keep growing or start declining?
faqs.a: Depends on where you sit. If your interest is tied to recent horizontal units on the eastern side, checks often ramp with new wells before settling into a decline curve typical of unconventional production. Legacy vertical wells on the western side tend to be past their growth phase and decline gradually. We factor your specific well history into any offer rather than guessing.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell everything, or can you sell part of your Pecos County interest?
faqs.a: You can sell all of it, a percentage, or even just the rights on a single well or unit while keeping the rest. Some owners sell a portion to get cash now while keeping a smaller royalty stream for the long run. We'll price whatever slice you're comfortable parting with.

faqs.q: How long does closing usually take on a Pecos County mineral sale?
faqs.a: With clean title, often two to four weeks. If there's a probate gap, an heirship issue, or an old unrecorded deed to sort out, it can run longer while the title company clears it. We tell you upfront which situation you're in before you commit to anything.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Culberson County, TX/NM
items.meta: Culberson County minerals sit in one of the deepest, richest parts of the Delaware Basin. Get a straight cash-offer conversation from a retired engineer.

sections.html:
Culberson County is remote even by West Texas standards, but the rock underneath it is some of the thickest, most stacked pay in the entire Delaware Basin.

We spent years working completions on Delaware Basin wells where the target zones sat deeper and the pressures ran higher than almost anywhere else in the Permian, and Culberson County was one of the counties where that showed up most clearly on the logs. The Bone Spring and Wolfcamp intervals here are thick enough that a single section can support multiple stacked landing zones, which is part of why big operators moved in aggressively over the last decade.

That intensity of development is good news if you own minerals or royalty in Culberson County, because it usually means more wells competing for the same acreage over time. It also means the interest can be genuinely complicated to value correctly, which is where we can help before you sign anything.

sections.title: A basin that got serious attention late
sections.html:
Culberson County didn't see meaningful horizontal drilling until well after Reeves and Loving counties to the north were already established, largely because the geology here runs deeper and the completions were more expensive to justify. Once operators proved the economics, though, Culberson became one of the more heavily permitted counties in the Delaware, with large public E&Ps building multi-well pad programs across big blocks of acreage.

That later start actually works in a mineral owner's favor in one specific way: much of the acreage here was leased and developed under more modern lease terms, with better royalty fractions and clearer Pugh clause language than you'd find on a lease signed in the 1970s. If your family's lease dates back further than that, it's still worth having us look at it, because older leases sometimes carry provisions that affect what a buyer will pay.

sections.title: What makes an offer higher or lower here
sections.html:
The biggest swing factor in Culberson County is how close your tract sits to the core development areas where multiple operators have already drilled and permitted stacked laterals. Acreage in the thick of that activity carries a different risk profile than acreage on the fringe where development is speculative, and we price accordingly rather than quoting one flat number for the whole county.

Decline stage matters too. A Wolfcamp well two years into production behaves very differently than one ten years in, and since Culberson's horizontal history is relatively young, a lot of the interests we see here are still on steep early decline curves. That's not a bad thing for value, it just means the numbers move faster than they would on an older, flatter-producing well, so we always want a recent check stub to see where the curve currently sits.

sections.title: Ownership realities in this part of the Delaware
sections.html:
A fair amount of Culberson County mineral ownership traces to large historic ranch holdings, sometimes with minerals split among an extended family or held inside a trust that was never fully wound down. If your interest comes through a trust or an estate that's still in some stage of probate, that doesn't stop us from making an offer, but it does affect the title work and the closing timeline.

We also regularly buy small non-operated working interests here, usually inherited alongside a royalty share. Working interest owners carry a portion of the drilling and operating costs, which is a very different risk than pure royalty, so if you're not sure which kind of interest you hold, send us the division order and we'll tell you plainly what you're looking at.

sections.title: Getting a real number, not a form-letter estimate
sections.html:
We don't send blind mailers quoting a per-acre number for Culberson County, because the range between a fringe undeveloped tract and a core-acreage producing interest is too wide for that to mean anything. Send us your division order, a recent check stub, or even just the section, block, and abstract number, and we'll pull what's publicly available and build a range specific to your interest.

This isn't tax or legal advice, and for questions about how a sale affects your estate or your tax return, talk to your CPA or attorney. What we offer is a candid conversation and a written offer with no obligation to move forward, and no pressure if the number isn't right for you.

faqs.q: Is Culberson County still an active area for new drilling?
faqs.a: Yes. It remains one of the more actively permitted counties in the Delaware Basin, with several large operators running multi-well pad development across stacked Wolfcamp and Bone Spring zones. That ongoing activity is a meaningful factor in how we value undeveloped or lightly developed acreage here.

faqs.q: your family's minerals are held in a trust, can you still buy the interest?
faqs.a: Generally yes. Trust-held interests just require the trustee to sign, and we'll ask for the trust documents to confirm who has authority. It adds a step to closing but doesn't prevent a sale.

faqs.q: Why would an offer on an undeveloped Culberson County tract be lower than a producing one?
faqs.a: An undeveloped tract has no current cash flow, so its value depends on the likelihood and timing of a future well. A producing interest has a visible decline curve we can analyze directly, which generally supports a stronger offer relative to a speculative tract.

faqs.q: Do you buy small fractional royalty interests in Culberson County?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's common here given how much acreage is split among heirs of larger historic ranch holdings. A small decimal interest under active development can still be worth a real offer.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Lea County, TX/NM
items.meta: Lea County, NM mineral owner? Between Hobbs, Jal and Lovington we've priced legacy Yeso wells and new Wolfcamp laterals alike. Get a direct offer, no listing needed.

sections.html:
Lea County has two faces: the Northwest Shelf shallow production around Lovington and Hobbs, and the Delaware Basin horizontal push toward the Texas line near Jal and Eunice.

Lea County produces more oil than any other county in New Mexico, and it's not close. That's not a marketing line, it's just what the state's own production numbers show, and it means the mineral ownership here is some of the most fought-over in the Permian. Between Hobbs, Jal, Lovington, Eunice and Monument you've got shallow San Andres and Yeso production going back to the 1930s stacked underneath a modern Bone Spring and Wolfcamp horizontal program.

That layering is exactly why two neighbors with adjoining tracts can get wildly different offers. One might be sitting on a section held by a 1960s vertical well paying almost nothing, the other under an active spacing unit with three or four horizontal laterals. We price the actual wellbore or unit you're in, county averages don't mean much here.

sections.title: The geology owners actually need to understand
sections.html:
Move west across Lea County from the Texas line and you cross from the Northwest Shelf onto the edge of the Delaware Basin proper. The shelf side, closer to Lovington and Tatum, produces from shallower San Andres and Yeso carbonate that's been on waterflood for decades in a lot of units. The basin side, toward Jal and the state line, is where the Bone Spring and Wolfcamp horizontal drilling has been concentrated for the last ten-plus years, with operators running multi-well pads on tight spacing.

If your family's minerals sit on the shelf side, don't assume you're missing out on the horizontal boom, plenty of shelf acreage still throws off steady, long-lived royalty income even without a new well. If you're on the basin side, your interest may be worth pursuing now specifically because of active permitting nearby.

sections.title: What drives our offer
sections.html:
We start with your division order or check stubs and pull the well or unit history from the New Mexico Oil Conservation Division. From there we're looking at decline rate, how many wells are actually on your unit versus permitted but not drilled, and whether there's competing acreage nearby that suggests more activity is coming. A tract with two producing horizontals and a permit filed on the offset section prices differently than one lone vertical well past its economic life.

We also see a lot of Lea County owners who inherited a working or royalty interest from a relative who worked in the oilfield here, sometimes going back to the original Hobbs field discovery era. Those interests often carry old, informal record-keeping, and we're used to reconstructing the chain of title from courthouse records rather than requiring you to have every document already in hand.

sections.title: Split estates and municipal overlap
sections.html:
Hobbs and Lovington have both grown enough that mineral tracts occasionally sit under developed or annexed land now, which raises surface-use questions the surface owner and mineral owner have to sort out separately from the sale. That doesn't stop a mineral sale, it's just something we flag early so there are no surprises at closing.

We also see a fair number of split estates where the surface was sold off generations ago but minerals stayed in the family. If that's your situation, your mineral interest is what we're buying, not the land, and the two are handled independently under New Mexico law.

faqs.q: Why would two tracts in the same section get different offers?
faqs.a: Because the specific wellbore or spacing unit each tract is pooled into matters more than the section itself. One unit might have active horizontal wells, the neighboring unit might still be held by a decades-old vertical well. We price against your actual unit's production, not a countywide estimate.

faqs.q: Is Lea County still an active drilling area or mostly legacy production now?
faqs.a: Both, depending where you are. The Delaware Basin side near Jal and the state line has ongoing horizontal Bone Spring and Wolfcamp activity. The Northwest Shelf side near Lovington and Tatum is more legacy San Andres and Yeso, though still economic in a lot of units.

faqs.q: You inherited a royalty interest and don't have most of the paperwork. Can you still make an offer?
faqs.a: Yes. We regularly reconstruct chain of title from the county clerk's records and NMOCD filings when an heir doesn't have the original documents in hand.

faqs.q: Does it matter that your minerals are under land inside city limits now?
faqs.a: Not for the mineral sale itself. Surface development and mineral ownership are separate under New Mexico law, though we'll flag any surface-use complications so you know what to expect at closing.

faqs.q: How do you value a working interest differently from a royalty interest?
faqs.a: A working interest carries a share of drilling and operating costs along with the production, so it's priced against net cash flow after those costs, not gross revenue like a royalty interest. Tell us which you hold and we'll run the numbers accordingly.

items.name: Sell Mineral Rights in Eddy County, TX/NM
items.meta: Eddy County, New Mexico sits at the heart of the Delaware Basin's most active drilling. Get a candid cash offer from a former E&P operations engineer.

sections.html:
If you had told us twenty years ago that Eddy County, New Mexico would become one of the hottest counties in the entire Permian, we'd have said you were thinking of the wrong state.

Eddy County runs the New Mexico side of the Delaware Basin story, centered on Carlsbad and stretching out through Artesia and a string of smaller communities that grew up around potash mining before oil ever mattered much here. Today it's a different picture entirely, with Bone Spring and Wolfcamp horizontal drilling running at a pace that rivals anything happening on the Texas side of the line.

Because New Mexico's regulatory and royalty framework differs from Texas in some meaningful ways, mineral owners here sometimes get valuations from Texas-focused buyers that don't quite fit. We've worked both sides of the state line long enough to price an Eddy County interest correctly, and we'll walk you through what actually matters.

sections.title: New Mexico's different rules matter for value
sections.html:
New Mexico state trust lands and federal BLM acreage make up a larger share of Eddy County than most Texas counties in this basin, and that affects both the pace of permitting and the royalty structure on a given unit. If your minerals sit under or near state or federal acreage, the surrounding development timeline can be different than a comparable tract just across the line in Texas.

New Mexico also handles spacing and pooling differently than Texas, and its statutory royalty rate on state leases can be higher than what you'd typically see negotiated privately. None of that changes the fundamentals of how we value your interest, but it's part of why we ask specifically which side of the state line and what kind of surface ownership sits above your minerals.

sections.title: Carlsbad, Artesia, and the acreage between them
sections.html:
The corridor between Carlsbad and Artesia has seen some of the most concentrated horizontal drilling in the entire Delaware Basin over the past several years, with major public operators running dense multi-well pad programs across large acreage blocks. Interests in that corridor tend to have more current production data and more visible future development to underwrite against.

Smaller communities scattered through the rest of the county, places like Atoka and Happy Valley, sit closer to the edges of that core activity, which doesn't mean the minerals are worthless, it just means we lean more heavily on nearby permitting trends than on your current check alone when we build a range.

sections.title: What builds a defensible offer
sections.html:
We look at net mineral acres, your specific decimal interest, the decline stage of producing wells, and permitted-but-undrilled locations nearby. Eddy County's active permitting pace means the third factor carries real weight here, since a well that hasn't spud yet can still meaningfully affect what a buyer is willing to pay for adjacent undeveloped minerals.

Values vary with commodity price and how close your tract sits to the current core development, so we won't quote a flat number without seeing the tract. What we will tell you is that a recent check stub or division order gets us to a real, specific range much faster than a guess based on the county name alone.

sections.title: Potash, ranching, and split mineral ownership
sections.html:

situations.title: Owner Situations Before a Sale

items.name: Got an Unsolicited Offer?
items.meta: Received a mailbox offer for your Permian Basin mineral or royalty rights? The Midland run sheet explains how to benchmark it before you sign anything.

sections.html:
A letter offering to buy your minerals showed up out of nowhere, and the number on it might be fair, low, or somewhere in between, and there's no way to know without checking it against something.

If you own Permian Basin minerals or royalty, you've probably gotten one of these letters, sometimes several a year from different companies, each offering a specific dollar figure to buy your interest, often with some urgency baked into the language. We've seen these letters from the buyer's side of the business, and we can tell you plainly: some are fair offers, some are lowball numbers hoping you don't check, and there's no way to tell which is which just by reading the letter itself.

You're under no obligation to respond quickly, or at all, and the single best thing you can do before signing anything is get a second read on what the offer actually represents against your interest's real production. We've reviewed plenty of these letters for owners who called us confused about the terms, and more than once the number turned out to be reasonable, which is exactly why a second opinion is worth getting either way rather than assuming the worst about every offer that shows up unsolicited.

sections.title: Why the same interest gets wildly different offers
sections.html:
Mailbox offers are often generated from public records and general county-level data, without the buyer having pulled your actual recent statements. That means the number can be based on assumptions about your specific well's decline rate, working interest, and net revenue interest that may not match reality at all, sometimes overestimating, sometimes underestimating what your interest is really producing.

A buyer working off your actual statements, rather than county-average assumptions, is going to land on a more accurate number, which is exactly why it's worth sharing your recent statements with more than one potential buyer before deciding anything.

Some letters are actually lease offers rather than purchase offers, seeking to lease your minerals rather than buy them outright, which is a completely different transaction with different implications for your long-term ownership. Read the letter carefully to understand which one you're actually looking at before responding.

sections.title: Red flags worth watching for
sections.html:
Be cautious of language pushing you to sign and return quickly, deadlines that expire in days rather than weeks, or an offer that arrives with a check already attached that becomes binding once cashed. None of these tactics are illegal, but they're designed to get you to act before you've compared the offer against anything else.

Also worth checking: does the letter clearly state whether they're offering to buy the mineral rights outright or just lease them, and whether the number quoted is per net mineral acre or some other basis. Vague language here is a sign to slow down, not speed up.

sections.title: How to actually benchmark an offer
sections.html:
Pull your recent statements, and if you can, the well name and API number off them. Share those with a second buyer, whether that's us or someone else, and ask for a straight comparison against the number you already received. You're not obligated to accept either offer, and getting a second opinion costs you nothing but a little time.

If the second number comes back close to the original offer, that's useful confirmation the first one was fair. If it comes back meaningfully higher, you've just saved yourself real money by not signing the first thing that showed up in the mail.

faqs.q: Should you sign the offer letter you got in the mail?
faqs.a: Not before comparing it against a second opinion. There's no downside to getting a benchmark quote before you decide, and reputable buyers won't pressure you to skip that step.

faqs.q: Why do mailbox offers vary so much between companies?
faqs.a: Many are generated from general public data rather than your actual current statements, which means the underlying assumptions about decline and interest size can differ significantly between buyers.

faqs.q: Is it legal to send unsolicited mineral rights purchase offers?
faqs.a: Yes, this is a common and legal practice in the industry. The offer itself being unsolicited doesn't say anything about whether the number is fair.

faqs.q: What information should you share to get a comparison offer?
faqs.a: Recent check stubs or division order statements, and the well name or lease name if you have it. That's usually enough for a real comparison.

faqs.q: Can you negotiate a mailbox offer instead of just accepting or rejecting it?
faqs.a: Yes, an initial offer is a starting point, not a final number. Sharing your actual production history with the sender can lead to a revised offer either way.

faqs.q: What's the difference between a purchase offer and a lease offer in the mail?
faqs.a: A purchase offer buys your mineral or royalty rights outright. A lease offer only grants drilling rights for a term while you retain ownership and future royalty. Read the letter closely to see which is being proposed.

faqs.q: Is it safe to give your Social Security number to respond to a mailbox offer?
faqs.a: Be cautious. Legitimate closings will eventually need identifying information for title and payment purposes, but that's typically handled later in the process, not upfront just to get a quote.

items.name: Inherited Mineral Rights
items.meta: Inherited Permian Basin mineral or royalty interests from a parent or grandparent? The Midland review team walks through what to check before deciding to keep or sell.

sections.html:
Most of the interests we buy in this basin didn't start with the person selling them, they started with a grandparent or great-grandparent who held onto West Texas ground long before the current drilling boom.

Inheriting mineral rights usually comes with more questions than answers. You might get a check every month or every quarter and have no idea what well it's tied to, or you might get nothing at all and wonder if the interest is even still active. Either way, the first step is the same: figure out exactly what you own before deciding what to do with it.

We've walked plenty of heirs through this, and the good news is that Permian counties keep decent records once you know where to look, even for interests that have sat quiet for years. Some of the more interesting positions we've bought started as a single county's worth of ranch land mineral rights, split evenly among five children two generations ago, and by the time it reached the current heirs it had become a scattered handful of fractional interests across several different wells and operators.

sections.title: Figuring out what you actually inherited
sections.html:
Start with the will or the probate order, which should describe the interest, though older documents sometimes just reference all mineral rights owned without listing specific tracts. If that's what you have, the county clerk's records in the relevant Permian county, cross-referenced against any division orders or check stubs that were being mailed to the deceased, will usually fill in the gaps.

If checks were coming in before your relative passed, contact the operator listed on the most recent statement and have the ownership transferred once probate closes. If nothing was being paid, that doesn't mean the interest is worthless, it may simply be sitting on non-producing acreage or land that hasn't been leased recently.

If your relative kept a file of old lease documents, division orders, or even handwritten notes about the property, hold onto everything, even paperwork that looks outdated. Old lease terms and legal descriptions are often exactly what's needed to confirm a chain of title that the county's own indexing might not make obvious at a glance.

sections.title: Deciding whether to keep or sell
sections.html:
Some heirs want to hold onto family mineral rights for sentimental reasons, and that's a legitimate call to make, especially if the interest is modest and low-maintenance. Others are dealing with multiple siblings, out-of-state addresses, and a small check that's more paperwork than it's worth, and selling cleans that up in one transaction.

There's no universally right answer here. What we'd say is don't decide based on assumptions about value either way. A quiet-looking interest can still be worth a real conversation, and a check that looks decent right now might be further into its decline than it appears.

sections.title: Multiple heirs, one interest
sections.html:
It's common for mineral rights to pass to several siblings or cousins jointly rather than to one person. If that's your situation, each heir typically has the right to sell their own undivided share independently, or the group can choose to sell together in a single transaction, which is usually simpler for everyone's paperwork.

If the family is split on what to do, that's fine too. We've closed plenty of deals where two siblings sold their shares and a third kept theirs, all off the same underlying interest, with no issue.

faqs.q: How do you find out what mineral rights you inherited in the Permian Basin?
faqs.a: Start with the probate documents and any check stubs your relative received, then check the deed records at the relevant county clerk's office to confirm the exact tract and interest size.

faqs.q: Do you have to sell your inherited mineral rights?
faqs.a: No, you can keep, lease, or sell an inherited interest, and each sibling or co-heir can typically make that choice independently for their own share.

faqs.q: What if you inherited mineral rights but never received a check?
faqs.a: That can mean the acreage isn't currently under a producing lease, or the operator doesn't have your updated ownership information yet. Both are worth following up on.

faqs.q: Is probate required before you can sell inherited minerals?
faqs.a: In most cases yes, the estate needs to be probated or an heirship affidavit accepted before a title company will clear the sale.

faqs.q: Can your siblings and you sell an inherited interest at different times?
faqs.a: Yes, each undivided co-owner generally controls their own share and can sell whenever they choose, independent of what other heirs decide to do.

faqs.q: What if you can't find any paperwork for minerals you believe you inherited?
faqs.a: Start with the county clerk's deed records in the relevant Permian county and search under your relative's name. Most transfers, including old ones, are recorded even if the family copy was lost.

faqs.q: Can you sell inherited mineral rights before they're formally retitled in your name?
faqs.a: Generally the title needs to reflect your ownership, typically through probate or an heirship affidavit, before a sale can close, so retitling usually comes first.

items.name: Minerals in Probate & Estates
items.meta: Executor or administrator handling Permian Basin mineral rights in an estate? The Midland run sheet explains valuation and the mechanics of an estate sale.

sections.html:
An executor's job is to settle the estate fairly, and that gets harder when one of the assets on the list is a mineral interest nobody else in the family fully understands.

When we get a call from an executor or estate administrator, it's usually because a mineral or royalty interest showed up in the inventory and nobody handling the estate has dealt with one before. That's normal. Most people aren't in the oil and gas business, and figuring out what an interest is worth while also managing every other estate asset is a lot to carry.

our job in that situation is straightforward: give you an honest, documented valuation you can use for the estate's records, and if the beneficiaries decide to sell rather than distribute the interest in kind, handle that sale cleanly within whatever the court or the will requires. We've worked with executors managing everything from a single small royalty interest to a scattered portfolio of mineral positions across four or five different Permian counties, all inherited from one estate, and the paperwork burden scales with that complexity fast.

sections.title: Why estates often sell rather than distribute minerals
sections.html:
Distributing a mineral interest among multiple beneficiaries means each one ends up with a small fractional share and their own ongoing division order relationship with the operator, which can be more administrative burden than any of them want, especially for a modest interest. Selling the interest as part of estate settlement and distributing cash instead is often simpler for everyone and avoids creating new fractional interests that get harder to manage with each generation.

That said, it's the beneficiaries' and executor's call, not ours. Some families do want to keep mineral rights in the family, and that's a legitimate choice when the interest is meaningful enough to justify it.

If the decedent held interests in multiple counties, expect to deal with more than one set of county records, since Texas probate matters are typically filed in the county of residence while the mineral records themselves sit in whatever county the acreage is actually located, which may be a different county entirely.

sections.title: What an estate needs for a clean valuation
sections.html:
For probate purposes, we'll need the same basics any buyer needs, recent statements or division order information, the legal description of the tract, and confirmation of the decedent's ownership, plus whatever the court requires to show the executor has authority to act, typically letters testamentary or letters of administration.

If the estate is going through independent administration in Texas, the process tends to move faster than dependent administration, which may require court approval for the sale itself. We've worked through both and can tell you early which situation you're in based on how the estate is being administered.

sections.title: Timing the sale against the estate's needs
sections.html:
Some estates need liquidity quickly, to cover final expenses, taxes, or an equal cash distribution among heirs who don't want to hold a shared mineral interest. Others are in less of a hurry and want the valuation on record while they finish administering everything else before deciding on a sale.

We can move at whatever pace the estate needs, whether that's a fast close to help settle final expenses or simply providing a documented offer the executor can hold onto and revisit once probate is further along.

faqs.q: Can an executor sell mineral rights before probate is finalized?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, once letters testamentary or letters of administration are issued, though it depends on whether the estate is under independent or dependent administration and what the will authorizes.

faqs.q: Do all beneficiaries have to agree to sell estate minerals?
faqs.a: If the executor has authority to sell as part of settling the estate, individual beneficiary consent for that sale isn't always required, though good practice is to keep everyone informed.

faqs.q: How is a mineral interest valued for estate and tax purposes?
faqs.a: Typically based on recent production history and current market conditions as of the date of death, which is different from a forward-looking sale price. We can provide documentation reflecting current value.

faqs.q: What documents does a buyer need from an executor?
faqs.a: Letters testamentary or administration, the death certificate, the will if applicable, and recent production statements or the deed showing the decedent's ownership.

faqs.q: Is selling minerals during probate faster than after distribution?
faqs.a: Often yes, because it avoids the extra step of retitling the interest into multiple heirs' names before a sale, which adds time and paperwork on the back end.

faqs.q: What if the decedent owned minerals in multiple Permian counties?
faqs.a: Each tract's ownership is confirmed through the deed records in its own county, even though the probate itself is typically administered in the decedent's county of residence.

faqs.q: Does the estate need a separate appraisal for each mineral interest?
faqs.a: Not necessarily separate appraisals, but each distinct interest generally needs its own valuation based on its specific production history, since they rarely share identical value even within the same estate.

image.alt: Minerals in Probate & Estates mineral rights

items.name: Fractional & Small Interests
items.meta: Own a tiny undivided fraction of Permian minerals with many other heirs on the same lease? The Midland run sheet explains what small interests are worth and why.

sections.html:
A 1/128th interest inherited four generations back is still real property, and it still shows up on a division order, even if the check barely covers a tank of gas.

Original allotments in West Texas were often split evenly among children, then split again among their children, and by the third or fourth generation an interest that started as a whole section is down to a fraction with a denominator nobody wants to write out. We see this constantly in Permian counties with a lot of old ranch land, where forty or fifty heirs can be listed on a single division order for one well.

Small doesn't mean worthless, but it does mean the interest behaves differently than a larger position, both in what it pays and in how much hassle it takes to keep track of. We've seen division orders in Reeves and Ward counties listing more than sixty separate heirs on a single legacy tract, each with their own tiny percentage, and untangling who's who is often the real work before any sale can close.

sections.title: Why tiny interests are expensive to hold
sections.html:
Every heir on a fractional interest gets their own division order, their own 1099, their own annual statement to track, sometimes from an operator that's changed hands two or three times since the original lease was signed. For an interest paying a few dollars a month, the administrative burden of keeping your address current, filing the tax paperwork, and fielding calls from every landman working that county can outweigh the actual income.

We've bought interests from heirs who told us the check itself wasn't the deciding factor, it was simply not wanting one more small account to manage alongside everything else in an estate that already has several moving pieces.

There's also a real cost on the operator's side to administering dozens of tiny accounts, cutting small checks, mailing 1099s, and fielding address-change requests every year, which is part of why some operators or buyers are willing to pay a modest premium to consolidate a fragmented ownership base into fewer, larger interests.

sections.title: How small interests get priced
sections.html:
A fractional interest is valued the same way a whole interest is, based on the well or wells it's tied to, current production, and remaining decline, just scaled down to your actual percentage. The math doesn't change because the number is small, though the total dollar figure obviously will be.

One thing worth knowing: buyers consolidating fractional interests in a single unit sometimes offer a modest premium for interests that help clean up a fragmented division order, especially if the operator has flagged the tract as hard to administer. It's not guaranteed, but it's worth asking about rather than assuming a small interest gets a worse rate proportionally.

sections.title: Clearing title on old, split interests
sections.html:
The biggest slowdown on fractional interests usually isn't the value, it's the paperwork. Interests that passed through multiple generations without a will, or through heirship affidavits instead of formal probate, can have title gaps that need to be cleared before a sale closes. If your interest traces back to a great-grandparent's original allotment, expect to spend some time confirming the chain of ownership.

We'll tell you upfront if your title looks clean or if it needs work before we can close, and we can point you toward what's typically needed, whether that's an heirship affidavit, a probate filing, or simply gathering the death certificates and family tree documentation a title company will ask for.

faqs.q: Is your fractional mineral interest worth selling if the check is only a few dollars?
faqs.a: Often the value is more about consolidating a small account and clearing paperwork than the check size alone. It's worth getting a read on the underlying well before deciding either way.

faqs.q: How many heirs can be on one division order?
faqs.a: It's common to see dozens of heirs listed on a single well in older Permian sections, especially where the original mineral owner's estate was never formally divided by deed.

faqs.q: Do you need probate to sell a fractional interest you inherited informally?
faqs.a: In many cases yes, unless the property already passed through a formal probate or an heirship affidavit that a title company will accept. This varies and is worth confirming early.

faqs.q: Can you sell just your fraction without the other heirs selling theirs?
faqs.a: Generally yes, undivided mineral interests can be sold individually by each owner without requiring the other co-owners to sell at the same time.

faqs.q: Will your fractional interest ever pay more if drilling picks up nearby?
faqs.a: It's possible if a new well is drilled on your unit, but a very small fractional interest will always produce a proportionally small check even in an active section.

faqs.q: What is the smallest mineral interest that's still worth selling?
faqs.a: There's no fixed cutoff, but very small fractional interests are usually worth evaluating anyway, since consolidating paperwork often matters as much to the owner as the dollar figure itself.

faqs.q: Do all heirs on a fractional interest have to sell together?
faqs.a: No, each heir generally holds an independent undivided share and can decide separately whether to keep or sell their portion, regardless of what other heirs choose.

image.alt: Fractional & Small Interests mineral rights

items.name: Leased but Undrilled
items.meta: Collected a lease bonus on Permian minerals but no well has been drilled yet? The Midland run sheet explains the lease clock, delay rentals, and your options.

sections.html:
A signed lease and a bonus check don't mean a well is coming next month, and we've talked to plenty of owners who are still waiting years after signing.

Getting a bonus payment for signing an oil and gas lease feels like the start of something, and sometimes it is, but plenty of leased Permian acreage sits untouched for the full primary term, or gets held by production on a neighboring unit without a well ever going on your specific tract. Understanding where your lease stands in its life cycle matters more than the bonus check you already cashed.

We've operated leases and we've bought interests still sitting in this exact spot, leased but quiet, and the questions we get are almost always the same: is this lease going to produce, and what is it worth if it doesn't. We've also seen owners assume a lease has quietly expired only to discover, once they check the county records, that it was extended years earlier through a delay rental or held by a nearby unit they didn't know their tract was pooled into.

sections.title: Understanding your lease's primary term
sections.html:
Most Permian leases run a primary term of three to five years, during which the operator has the exclusive right to drill without being obligated to. If a well isn't drilled and the lease isn't held by production or extended through a delay rental payment, it expires at the end of that term and the mineral rights revert fully to you, free of any lease.

Check your lease document for the exact primary term and any delay rental clause. Some leases require an annual payment to keep the lease alive without drilling, others don't, and knowing which kind you signed tells you whether silence from the operator means they've moved on or simply haven't gotten to your tract yet.

Some leases also include a Pugh clause, which limits how much of a large tract can be held by production from a small portion actually being drilled. If your lease has one, it's worth understanding, since it can mean part of your acreage reverts to you even while another part stays held by an existing well.

sections.title: Held by production on a pooled unit
sections.html:
In this basin, your specific tract doesn't need a wellbore on it to be held by production. If your acreage is pooled into a unit with a well drilled elsewhere in that unit, the whole unit, including your tract, can be held indefinitely even though no well ever touches your specific acres. That's normal and it's worth checking the pooling or unitization records at the county clerk to see if that's your situation.

If your tract is held by production this way, you may already be entitled to royalty from the pooled well even without a well on your specific parcel, depending on how the pooling was structured. It's worth confirming with the operator directly whether you're being paid correctly.

sections.title: What leased-but-undrilled acreage is worth
sections.html:
A leased, undrilled interest carries potential value tied to how active the surrounding area is and how much lease term remains. A tract with two years left on the primary term in a county seeing active permitting nearby is a very different proposition than one with six months left in a quiet area where the operator seems to have stopped filing permits.

We'll look at your lease terms, the county activity around your tract, and whether there's real reason to think drilling is coming, and give you an honest read on whether the interest is worth more held or sold now, rather than pushing one direction regardless of what the facts show.

faqs.q: What happens to your minerals if the lease expires without a well being drilled?
faqs.a: The lease terminates and the mineral rights revert to you free and clear, at which point you're able to lease again to a new or the same operator on new terms.

faqs.q: Can you sell mineral rights that are currently leased but not producing?
faqs.a: Yes, you can sell the underlying mineral or royalty interest even while a lease is in place. The buyer takes over your position subject to that existing lease.

faqs.q: Why is your leased tract not being drilled while nearby tracts are?
faqs.a: Operators sequence drilling based on their own development plans, spacing units, and permitting priorities, which don't always follow lease boundaries or timelines an individual owner can predict.

faqs.q: Is a delay rental payment the same as a royalty?
faqs.a: No, a delay rental is a payment to keep an undrilled lease alive during its primary term. Royalty only begins once a well on your unit is actually producing.

faqs.q: Should you wait out the lease term or sell now?
faqs.a: It depends on how much term is left and how active the surrounding county is. We'll give you a straight read on your specific lease rather than a generic answer.

faqs.q: What is a Pugh clause and does your lease have one?
faqs.a: A Pugh clause limits how much acreage stays held by production from a single well, protecting undrilled portions of a larger tract from being held indefinitely. Check your lease document for this language directly.

faqs.q: Can an operator extend your lease without drilling by paying a delay rental?
faqs.a: Yes, if your lease includes a delay rental clause, the operator can keep the lease alive through the primary term with that payment instead of actually drilling a well.

image.alt: Leased but Undrilled mineral rights

items.name: Non-Producing Minerals
items.meta: Own Permian Basin acreage with no current wells or an expired lease? The Midland run sheet explains what drives value on non-producing minerals and what to expect.

sections.html:
No check doesn't mean no value, but it does mean the conversation about your minerals looks different than it would for a producing tract.

Plenty of mineral owners in this basin hold acreage that's never been drilled, or was leased and drilled decades ago on a well that's since plugged, or sits between active units without a permit filed against it yet. That's non-producing acreage, and it's a completely different animal to value than an interest with a check history behind it.

We get calls from owners who assume quiet acreage is worthless and others who assume it must be valuable simply because it's in the Permian. Neither assumption is reliable. What matters is what's happening on the ground around your specific tract. We also look at whether a tract has ever been leased at all versus leased and then let expire, since a history of prior leasing interest, even without a well, tells us something different than acreage that's never drawn attention from any operator.

sections.title: What makes non-producing acreage valuable
sections.html:
The biggest driver is proximity to current activity. Acreage sitting inside or adjacent to an active spacing unit, in a county where operators are actively permitting and drilling, carries real speculative value even with zero production history, because a lease or a future well is a realistic possibility, not a hypothetical.

Acreage in a quiet part of a county, away from recent permits, with no operator activity nearby in the last several years, is a harder sell. It's still your property and it still has some value, but that value is smaller and more speculative, and we'll tell you that directly rather than talk around it.

Formation depth matters here too. Some non-producing Permian acreage sits over multiple stacked intervals that simply haven't been targeted yet with current lateral lengths and completion designs, which is different from acreage over a thinner, less prospective section that's genuinely been passed over for good geological reasons.

sections.title: Expired leases and what comes next
sections.html:
If your tract was leased and drilled years ago and the well has since been plugged and abandoned, or the lease simply expired without ever being drilled, your minerals are unencumbered and available to lease again. Whether a new operator is interested depends heavily on current commodity pricing and whether the geology under your specific tract is still considered prospective with modern drilling and completion techniques.

Some formations that weren't economic to drill with older technology are being revisited now with longer laterals and different completion designs, so a tract that went quiet a decade ago isn't necessarily permanently off the table.

sections.title: How we evaluate a non-producing tract
sections.html:
We pull recent permit activity within a mile or two of your acreage, check who's operating nearby, and look at whether any pooling or unitization filings touch your section. That tells us whether your tract is realistically in the path of near-term development or sitting well outside it.

If the picture looks active, we'll make an offer reflecting that speculative potential. If it doesn't, we'll say so plainly rather than make a lowball offer dressed up as a fair one. Sometimes the honest answer is that it's not the right time to sell, and we'd rather tell you that than waste your time.

faqs.q: Are non-producing mineral rights worth anything?
faqs.a: Yes, but the value is speculative and tied to nearby drilling activity rather than an existing check. Acreage near active development can still be worth real money even with zero production.

faqs.q: Can you lease your minerals again if the old lease expired?
faqs.a: Yes, once a lease expires without production, your rights are unencumbered and available to lease to a new operator, subject to current market interest in your area.

faqs.q: How do you know if your non-producing acreage is near active drilling?
faqs.a: County permit records, available through the Railroad Commission and the county clerk, show recent filings. We check this before making any offer on quiet acreage.

faqs.q: Why would someone buy minerals with no production history?
faqs.a: Buyers interested in speculative acreage are betting on future drilling potential based on nearby activity, similar to buying undeveloped land near a growing area.

faqs.q: Is it better to hold non-producing minerals and wait?
faqs.a: It depends on how active the surrounding area is and your own timeline. We'll give you an honest read on your specific tract's activity level before you decide.

faqs.q: How do you check if your non-producing acreage has ever been leased before?
faqs.a: The county clerk's real property records will show any historical oil and gas leases filed against your tract, including ones that have since expired.

faqs.q: Will a landman contact you if your non-producing acreage becomes interesting to operators?
faqs.a: Often yes, landmen actively research county records and reach out to mineral owners in areas with rising activity, though you don't have to wait for that call to get your own read on the tract.

faqs.q: Does owning non-producing minerals cost you anything to keep?
faqs.a: Generally no ongoing cost is required simply to hold non-producing mineral rights. You're not liable for property taxes or maintenance on the minerals themselves, since those obligations sit with whoever owns the surface, not the mineral estate.

faqs.q: What's the fastest way to check current permit activity near your non-producing tract?
faqs.a: The Railroad Commission of Texas maintains an online permit database searchable by county and survey. Cross-referencing that against your legal description gives a reasonably current picture of nearby activity without needing to hire anyone.

image.alt: Non-Producing Minerals mineral rights

items.name: Trust-Owned Minerals
items.meta: Trustee managing Permian Basin mineral or royalty interests inside a trust? The Midland review team on fiduciary duty, valuation, and the sale process for trustees.

sections.html:
A trustee has a duty to the beneficiaries that goes beyond just collecting a check, and that duty is exactly why trust-owned minerals deserve a more careful look than most.

Mineral rights held in a family trust come with a layer that a personally owned interest doesn't: the trustee's fiduciary obligation to manage the asset prudently for the beneficiaries, whether that's one surviving spouse, a group of adult children, or a trust set up for minors that won't distribute for years.

We've worked with trustees who are professional fiduciaries and trustees who are simply the oldest sibling who got named in the document, and the questions are usually the same: is the trust getting fair value from this interest, and does it make more sense to hold it or sell it. We've also worked with corporate trustees at banks and trust companies who need a documented, defensible valuation on file simply as a matter of standard fiduciary practice, separate from any active decision about whether to sell.

sections.title: The trustee's duty on mineral assets
sections.html:
Prudent management of a mineral interest generally means staying informed about production, making sure royalty is being paid correctly, and periodically evaluating whether continuing to hold the interest still serves the trust's purpose and the beneficiaries' interests, especially for a trust with a defined term or a specific income mandate.

Documentation matters here more than in a personal sale. A trustee should be able to show, if ever asked, that a decision to sell was based on a fair, current valuation rather than an arbitrary number, and we provide the documentation to support that.

Special needs trusts and trusts for minor beneficiaries carry an extra layer of caution, since the trustee's obligations often extend well beyond ordinary prudent investor standards. If your trust falls into either category, involve the trust's attorney early, before any valuation or sale discussion goes very far.

sections.title: When selling makes sense for a trust
sections.html:
Trusts with income mandates sometimes benefit from converting a volatile, declining royalty stream into a lump sum that can be reinvested into more predictable income-generating assets, which can better match what the trust document actually requires the trustee to provide beneficiaries. A small, hard-to-administer fractional interest can also be more trouble than it's worth relative to the trust's overall size.

On the other hand, some trusts are specifically structured to hold mineral assets long-term, and selling would run against the settlor's intent. That's a call the trustee makes with the trust document and, where appropriate, legal counsel, not something we'd ever push one way or the other on.

sections.title: What we need from a trustee to move forward
sections.html:
We'll need the trust document, or at least the certification of trust showing the trustee's authority to sell, recent production statements, and the deed or prior conveyance showing the trust's ownership. If there are co-trustees, we'll need to understand whether both need to sign or one has independent authority.

From there the process runs the same as any other sale, just with the trust's documentation standing in for an individual owner's, and we're used to working within whatever review process a trustee needs to follow before authorizing a transaction like this.

faqs.q: Can a trustee sell mineral rights without beneficiary approval?
faqs.a: It depends on the trust document. Many trusts give the trustee independent authority to sell assets, but some require beneficiary consent or court approval, so check your specific document.

faqs.q: What documents does a trustee need to sell mineral rights?
faqs.a: The trust document or certification of trust, recent production statements, and the deed showing the trust's ownership are the core pieces needed to move forward.

faqs.q: Is a trustee liable if they sell minerals below market value?
faqs.a: A trustee can face liability for failing to meet fiduciary duty, which is why documenting a fair, current valuation before selling matters for the trustee's own protection.

faqs.q: Should a trust hold or sell a declining mineral interest?
faqs.a: It depends on the trust's purpose and income requirements. A declining, volatile royalty stream may not match a trust mandate for stable income as well as a lump sum reinvested elsewhere would.

faqs.q: Can co-trustees disagree on selling a mineral interest?
faqs.a: It's possible, and how that's resolved depends on the trust document's rules about co-trustee authority. Some require unanimous agreement, others allow majority or independent action.

faqs.q: Does a corporate trustee at a bank need a different process than an individual trustee?
faqs.a: The underlying valuation and sale mechanics are the same, though corporate trustees often have internal approval processes and documentation standards that add steps before a sale is authorized.

faqs.q: How often should a trustee revalue mineral assets held in trust?
faqs.a: There's no fixed rule, but many trustees revisit valuations periodically, especially after a significant change in production, commodity prices, or nearby drilling activity.

faqs.q: Can a successor trustee sell minerals the original trustee never addressed?
faqs.a: Yes, once a successor trustee is properly appointed under the trust document, they generally inherit the same authority the original trustee held, including the ability to evaluate and sell trust assets like mineral interests.

faqs.q: Does the trust need its own tax identification number to receive sale proceeds?
faqs.a: Most trusts already have an EIN for tax reporting purposes, and that same number is typically used to receive proceeds from a mineral sale, separate from any individual beneficiary's Social Security number.

image.alt: Trust-Owned Minerals mineral rights

items.name: Out-of-State Owners
items.meta: Managing Permian Basin mineral or royalty interests from out of state? The Midland review team on tracking checks, operator changes, and selling from a distance.

sections.html:
Owning West Texas minerals from another state usually means finding out about operator changes, lease offers, or drilling permits later than everyone standing on the ground.

A lot of the interests we buy belong to people who've never set foot in the Permian counties where their minerals sit. They inherited the position, or a relative moved away decades ago and the mineral rights just stayed behind, and now they're managing an asset in Texas or New Mexico from California, Florida, or wherever life took them.

That distance creates real friction. Mail gets missed, operator changes go unnoticed, and by the time an out-of-state owner hears about activity near their tract, local owners and landmen already know the full picture. We've closed deals with owners in nearly every corner of the country who hold Permian minerals through a grandparent who moved away from West Texas decades ago, and the story is almost always the same: the interest stayed behind while the family didn't.

sections.title: The information gap is real
sections.html:
Operators typically send division order statements and 1099s to whatever address is on file, but they don't proactively call to explain what's happening with your interest. If a well near your tract goes into decline, or a new operator takes over the lease, or a pooling order gets filed, you're finding that out from a mailed statement, if at all, well after local owners have already heard through word of mouth.

This is one of the biggest reasons out-of-state owners end up selling: not because the interest is bad, but because staying informed enough to manage it well from a distance is genuinely harder than it looks.

It's also worth knowing that some states have unclaimed property laws requiring operators to turn over royalty payments to the state after a period of undeliverable mail, sometimes as short as a few years. Recovering funds from a state's unclaimed property division is possible but adds an extra step most owners would rather avoid entirely.

sections.title: Keeping your address and paperwork current
sections.html:
If you've moved, or inherited an interest with an old address still on file, update it with the operator directly. Missed statements can mean missed income, and in some states unclaimed royalty payments eventually get turned over to the state's unclaimed property division, which means additional paperwork to recover money that was rightfully yours all along.

Keep copies of your deed, any lease documents, and recent statements in one place, physical or digital, so that whenever you do decide to sell or need to prove ownership, you're not searching for documents that got lost in a move or an inherited filing cabinet.

sections.title: Selling long-distance, start to finish
sections.html:
You don't need to travel to Texas or New Mexico to sell a mineral or royalty interest. We handle the entire process by phone, email, and mail, including notarized documents that can be signed at any local notary near you, with funds wired or mailed once title is confirmed.

For a lot of out-of-state owners, that's the appeal: closing out an asset that's been more distant hassle than benefit, without needing to fly anywhere or deal with a local closing in person.

faqs.q: Do you need to travel to Texas to sell your mineral rights?
faqs.a: No, the entire process, including signing and notarizing documents, can be handled remotely from wherever you live.

faqs.q: How do you find out if your mineral rights are still active from out of state?
faqs.a: Contact the operator listed on your most recent statement, or check the county clerk's records in the relevant Permian county, which are often searchable online now.

faqs.q: What if your royalty checks stopped and you don't know why?
faqs.a: It could mean the well went into a state where escheat or unclaimed property rules apply if the operator lost your current address, or it could reflect a real decline or operational issue. Worth checking both.

faqs.q: Is it harder to sell an out-of-state mineral interest?
faqs.a: Not really, distance doesn't change the underlying value of the interest, and the closing process is designed to work by mail and phone for exactly this situation.

faqs.q: Should you hire someone local in Texas to manage your interest?
faqs.a: Some owners do use a local landman or attorney for ongoing management, but for many out-of-state owners with a modest interest, selling outright ends up being the simpler path.

faqs.q: How do you claim royalty payments that were turned over to a state's unclaimed property division?
faqs.a: Most states have a searchable unclaimed property database. You'll typically need to file a claim with documentation proving your identity and ownership, which can take several weeks to process.

faqs.q: Can a family member local to Texas manage your mineral interest for you?
faqs.a: Yes, some owners grant a local family member or attorney power of attorney to handle correspondence and paperwork, though this isn't required to keep the interest properly managed.

faqs.q: How do out-of-state heirs typically split an inherited Permian interest?
faqs.a: Each heir usually receives an undivided fractional share and can decide independently whether to keep, lease, or sell their portion, regardless of where the other heirs live or what they choose to do with theirs.

faqs.q: Will you need a notary in your own state to sell from out of state?
faqs.a: Yes, closing documents can typically be signed before any licensed notary near you, then mailed back, so you don't need to find one specifically in Texas or New Mexico.

image.alt: Out-of-State Owners mineral rights

items.name: Selling for Liquidity
items.meta: Need cash from Permian Basin mineral or royalty rights for medical bills, retirement, or debt? The Midland review team on getting a fair, fast valuation.

sections.html:
When you need cash now, a monthly royalty check that trickles in over years doesn't solve the problem in front of you, and that's a completely legitimate reason to consider a sale.

Not every mineral sale is about estate planning or inherited complexity. A lot of the calls we get are from owners facing something more immediate, medical bills that need to be paid, retirement income that needs a lump sum behind it, or debt that a steady but small monthly check isn't going to resolve fast enough.

We don't need to know your full financial picture to give you a fair, honest valuation, but understanding that liquidity is the goal helps us focus on what actually matters to you: a clean number and a fast, reliable close, rather than drawing the process out. We try to move quickly once we understand the situation is time-sensitive, because we've been on the other side of financial pressure ourselves and we know that a slow, drawn-out process can be its own kind of burden on top of whatever prompted the sale in the first place.

sections.title: Royalty income versus a lump sum
sections.html:
A royalty check represents a stream of future income, discounted down to a single present value when you sell. That discount reflects real uncertainty, commodity prices move, wells decline, and a dollar received today is worth more than the same dollar spread out over the next several years. Understanding that tradeoff upfront helps you decide whether a lump sum makes more sense for your situation than continuing to collect monthly or quarterly checks.

For someone facing a real, current need, a smaller lump sum now often outweighs a larger total amount collected slowly over years, especially when interest on debt or the cost of delaying a medical decision is part of the equation.

Medical expenses in particular tend to arrive without much warning, and a royalty check that pays a few hundred dollars a month simply isn't built to absorb a large, immediate bill. Converting that stream to a lump sum, even a modest one, can make a real difference when the need is measured in weeks, not years.

sections.title: How fast a sale can actually close
sections.html:
Once we have your recent statements, the deed, and confirmation of clear title, a straightforward Permian Basin mineral or royalty sale can often close within a few weeks. Complications like unclear title, multiple heirs who haven't all been contacted, or an estate that hasn't finished probate will add time, so it's worth flagging any of those issues early rather than discovering them mid-process.

If speed matters most to you, tell us that directly. We'll let you know honestly whether your specific situation is likely to move fast or whether there's a real obstacle to clear first.

sections.title: Selling part of your interest instead of all of it
sections.html:
You don't have to sell your entire interest to solve a liquidity need. Some owners sell a percentage, or sell the rights to a set number of years of production, keeping a smaller ongoing interest while still getting the cash they need now. This isn't right for every situation, but it's worth knowing it's an option rather than assuming a sale is all-or-nothing.

We'll walk through both structures with you plainly, a full sale versus a partial sale, so you can decide which actually fits what you need rather than defaulting to whichever is easier for us to process.

faqs.q: How fast can you get cash from selling your Permian royalty?
faqs.a: With clear title and recent statements in hand, a straightforward sale can often close within a few weeks from first contact to funds received.

faqs.q: Can you sell just part of your mineral interest instead of all of it?
faqs.a: Yes, partial sales, either a percentage of the interest or a defined term of production, are an option if you want some liquidity while keeping ongoing income.

faqs.q: Will selling your royalty affect your taxes?
faqs.a: A mineral sale is generally treated differently than ongoing royalty income for tax purposes. Talk to your CPA or tax advisor about how a sale affects your specific situation.

faqs.q: Is selling for immediate cash a bad deal compared to waiting?
faqs.a: It depends on your situation and how much you value certainty now versus a potentially larger but uncertain total collected over years. There's no universally right answer.

faqs.q: Do you need good credit or approval to sell mineral rights?
faqs.a: No, selling a mineral or royalty interest isn't a loan or credit transaction, it's a sale of real property you already own, so credit isn't part of the process.

faqs.q: Can you get an advance or partial payment before the full sale closes?
faqs.a: In some urgent situations this can be arranged once title is confirmed clear, though it depends on the specifics. Ask directly if timing is critical for you.

faqs.q: Will selling your mineral rights affect eligibility for benefits like Medicaid?
faqs.a: A lump sum from a mineral sale could affect asset-based eligibility for certain programs. Talk to a benefits or elder law specialist before selling if this applies to you.

image.alt: Selling for Liquidity mineral rights

items.name: Mineral Rights in Divorce
items.meta: Splitting Permian Basin royalty or mineral interests in a divorce settlement? The Midland run sheet explains valuation, buyouts, and clean ways to divide or sell.

sections.html:
A royalty interest doesn't split evenly the way a bank account does, and we've watched more than one settlement stall over what a Permian mineral position is actually worth.

When minerals or royalty come up in a divorce, the two sides usually don't disagree about who owns what on paper, they disagree about the number.
